title: Ecclesiasticus, or the Wisdom of Jesus, Son of Sirach
text:
51
PRAYER OF JESUS SON OF SIRACHg


I give you thanks, O Lord and King,
  and praise you, O God my Savior.
I give thanks to your name,
  2for you have been my protector and helper
and have delivered me from destruction
  and from the trap laid by a slanderous tongue,
from lips that fabricate lies.
  In the face of my adversaries
you have been my helper 3and delivered me,
  in the greatness of your mercy and of your name,
from grinding teeth about to devour me,
  from the hand of those seeking my life,
  from the many troubles I endured,
4from choking fire on every side,
  and from the midst of fire that I had not kindled,
5from the deep belly of Hades,
  from an unclean tongue and lying words—
  6the slander of an unrighteous tongue to the king.
My soul drew near to death,
  and my life was on the brink of Hades below.
7They surrounded me on every side,
  and there was no one to help me;
I looked for human assistance,
  and there was none.
8Then I remembered your mercy, O Lord,
  and your kindnessh from of old,
for you rescue those who wait for you
  and save them from the hand of their enemies.
9And I sent up my prayer from the earth,
  and begged for rescue from death.
10I cried out, “Lord, you are my Father;i
  do not forsake me in the days of trouble,
  when there is no help against the proud.
11I will praise your name continually,
  and will sing hymns of thanksgiving.”
My prayer was heard,
  12for you saved me from destruction
  and rescued me in time of trouble.
For this reason I thank you and praise you,
  and I bless the name of the Lord.





                 
Heb Adds:


Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to the God of praises,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to the guardian of Israel,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to him who formed all things,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to the redeemer of Israel,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to him who gathers the dispersed of Israel,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to him who rebuilt his city and his sanctuary,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to him who makes a horn to sprout for the house of David,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to him who has chosen the sons of Zadok to be priests,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to the shield of Abraham,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to the rock of Isaac,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to the mighty one of Jacob,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to him who has chosen Zion,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


Give thanks to the King of the kings of kings,
  for his steadfast love endures forever;


He has raised up a horn for his people,
  praise for all his loyal ones.


For the children of Israel, the people close to him.
  Praise the Lord!

                 

13While I was still young, before I went on my travels,
  I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.
14Before the temple I asked for her,
  and I will search for her until the end.


15From the first blossom to the ripening grape
  my heart delighted in her;
my foot walked on the straight path;
  from my youth I followed her steps.


16I inclined my ear a little and received her,
  and I found for myself much instruction.
17I made progress in her;
  to him who gives wisdom I will give glory.


18For I resolved to live according to wisdom,a
  and I was zealous for the good,
  and I shall never be disappointed.
19My soul grappled with wisdom,a
  and in my conduct I was strict;b


I spread out my hands to the heavens,
  and lamented my ignorance of her.
20I directed my soul to her,
  and in purity I found her.


With her I gained understanding from the first;
  therefore I will never be forsaken.
21My heart was stirred to seek her;
  therefore I have gained a prize possession.
22The Lord gave me my tongue as a reward,
  and I will praise him with it.


23Draw near to me, you who are uneducated,
  and lodge in the house of instruction.
24Why do you say you are lacking in these things,a
  and why do you endure such great thirst?
25I opened my mouth and said,
  Acquire wisdomb for yourselves without money.


26Put your neck under herc yoke,
  and let your souls receive instruction;
  it is to be found close by.


27See with your own eyes that I have labored but little
  and found for myself much serenity.
28Hear but a little of my instruction,
  and through me you will acquire silver and gold.d


29May your soul rejoice in God'se mercy,
  and may you never be ashamed to praise him.
30Do your work in good time,
  and in his own time Godf will give you your reward.





Prologue: Ben Sira's grandson composed a Prologue to the Greek translation that accompanies modern translations, since they are, for the most part, based on the Greek. In three elegant sentences (coinciding with the paragraphs in this translation), he tells about Ben Sira and his reason for writing, his own motivation for translating, and the difficulties of translating from Hebrew into Greek. He divides the literary heritage of Israel into three categories, two specific and one vague: the Law and the Prophets and the other books. Jesus is the Gk form of Heb “Yeshua,” which appears in 50.27 in a Hebrew manuscript (MS B). Instruction and wisdom could refer to the combination of Torah and proverbial wisdom characteristic of Ben Sira's book. The thirty-eighth year of the reign of Euergetes, 132 bce. Most scholars think that Ben Sira's grandson finished his translation somewhere shortly after Euergetes's death in 117 bce. The translation was for the Jewish community living abroad in Egypt so that they could benefit from his grandfather's wisdom. Note how he parallels language about his grandfather's intent with his own: love learning/gain learning; live according to the law.



1.1–10: Praise of Wisdom. God created Wisdom (Gk “sophia,” a feminine noun), which is probably meant to be a feminine figure, and gave her as a gift to all creation. 2–6: The rhetorical questions assume a negative answer, i.e., no human can know creation's secrets (cf. Job 38–39). 4: Created before all things, cf. 24.1–7; Prov 8.22–26; Wis 7.24–26. 9–10: Wisdom is a double gift, given to all his works, as well as specifically to those who love him (cf. Job 28.23–28).


1.11–30: Fear of the Lord is wisdom. Ben Sira establishes his three main theological themes in this poem: wisdom, fear of the Lord, and keeping the commandments, which are found in the Torah (24.23). 11: Fear of the Lord, the proper response to God's gift is awe and proper conduct (cf. Prov 1.7). 12: God rewards those who fear the Lord with long life, desirable goods (v. 17), and perfect health (v. 18); cf. v. 20; Prov 3.16; 22.4. 13: Happy end, immortality for Ben Sira consists primarily in leaving behind righteous children, along with a good name and reputation (40.19; 41.11–13). 14: Beginning of wisdom, Prov 1.7; 9.10; Ps 111.10. In the womb, a prophetic motif (49.7; Jer 1.5; Isa 44.2,24; 49.1,5; cf. Ps 139.13; Gal 1.15). 16: Wisdom is apportioned to all humans (cf. v. 19). 19: Heightened the glory of those who held her fast, see 24.19. 20: Wisdom is often pictured with imagery of plants, especially as a tree of life; see 24.13–17 (cf. Gen 3.22). 30: Before the whole congregation emphasizes Ben Sira's concern for honor and shame.


2.1–18: Trusting in God. How to remain faithful to God. 1: My child, lit., “my son,” a common way to refer to students in instructional literature (e.g., 3.17; 4.1; Prov 1.8; 2.1). 4–6: One must persevere in time of testing (v. 1), which is akin to refining gold (Prov 17.3; 27.21; Wis 3.6). 7–9: The threefold repetition of fear of the Lord (see 1.11n.) emphasizes wait, trust, and hope; see also vv. 15–17. 10: An appeal to the past to prove that trusting God brings reward (cf. Job 4.7; 8.8–10). 11: The Lord is compassionate and merciful, Ex 34.6–7; Ps 103.8; Jon 4.2. 12–14: The woe is a prophetic form, here used as a warning. The Lord's reckoning refers to recompense in this life. 15–16: His words and his ways are synonyms for his law. 18: Fall into the hands of the Lord, 2 Sam 24.14. Name, a reference to God as “Merciful One” (50.19).


3.1–16: Duties to parents. 1–2: God made the family hierarchical with parents above children. For the father as family head, see 7.23–26. On respect for both parents, see, e.g., Prov 1.8–9; 6.20; 20.20; 23.22; Ex 20.12; 21.15,17. 3–7: Honoring parents atones for sins (vv. 3,14; as do almsgiving and sacrifice; see 3.30; cf. 28.1–5) and brings long life (Ex 20.12; Deut 5.16). It thus equals fear of the Lord (1.12). 8–11: For the significance of a father's blessing, see Gen 27.1–29; 48.15–20; 49.1–28. Dishonoring parents brings disgrace, that is, shame. 16: The invoking of a blasphemer emphasizes that true piety is keeping God's commandments.


3.17–29: Humility. 17–20: Humility is a marker of piety (1.27) and so wins God's favor. 21: What is too difficult may refer to Jewish apocalyptic or Greek philosophical ideas about the secrets of creation; cf. Prov 30.18. 22: Wisdom and knowledge come from what is commanded (the Torah) and the proverbs (v. 29) of the sages, two foundational sources of wisdom for Ben Sira.


3.30–4.10: Almsgiving. 30–31: Atones for sin, cf. 3.3–4,14. 4.1–5: Ben Sira belongs to a class that has resources to help the needy, which the law commands (Deut 15.7–11). 6: Curse, cf. Ex 22.22–24; Deut 15.9. 10: On care for the widow and the orphan, see, e.g., Ex 22.22.


4.11–19: Submission to Wisdom. Wisdom's benefits are acquired through discipline. As in Prov 1.8–33; 8; Sir 24, Wisdom is personified as a woman. 14: Minister alludes to priestly service (cf. 24.10 regarding Wisdom). Holy One, a frequent title for God in Sirach (23.9; 43.10; 47.8; 48.20). 16: Faithful to Wisdom's teaching. 17–19: Wisdom's trials test the student's steadfastness. The term ordinances brings Torah and Wisdom together, anticipating Sir 24. 18: Reveal, acquiring wisdom has a revelatory aspect; cf. 39.7. 19: Cf. v. 16.


4.20–31: Shame and speech. An extended sequence of negative admonitions (do not) is a common stylistic feature in wisdom literature (see also 1.28–30; 4.1–6; 5; 7.1–26; cf. Prov 3.27–32). 20–21: For specifics on improper and proper shame, see 41.17–42.8. 23–26: Appropriate speech is a frequent topic in Sirach as well as in Jewish wisdom literature; cf. 19.6–17; 20.16–20; 22.27–23.15; 28.12–26; Prov 10.19; 12.6; 17.4. 26: Stop the current of a river, a metaphor for the impossibility of hiding sins from God. 28: Showing partiality to a ruler might require compromising one's integrity; see 7.6. 30: Lion, a frequent image in Sirach for ferocity (21.2; 25.16; 27.10,28; 28.23).


5.1–8: Avoid presumption. Do not presume that God will overlook sins. 1: Ben Sira is preoccupied with wealth, its acquisition, and use (5.8; 10.30; 14.3; 28.10; 31.1; 40.13). 4–6: See the liturgical formula in Ex 34.6–7 (and its later adaptations, e.g., Num 14.18; Pss 86.15; 103.8; 145.8) where God is slow to anger and shows mercy. Here, though, rather than as part of a promise, Ben Sira warns that God also brings wrath on the guilty. Cf. Sir 16.11–14. 7–8: For the sudden onset of calamity as punishment, see Prov 6.15; 24.22.


5.9–6.4: Speech, shame, and passion. 10: See 4.23–26n. 12: Hand over your mouth, a gesture of silence, humility, and submission (Job 29.9; 40.4; Prov 30.32). 14: Double-tongued, duplicitous or slandering (6.1; 28.13). 6.1: A bad name incurs shame shows the importance of reputation for Ben Sira (15.1–10; 37.26; 39.9,11; 40.19; 41.11–13; 44.1–15). 6.2–4: The transparent sexual image, withered tree, is the consequence of the grip of passion.


6.5–17: Friendship. One must exercise caution when choosing friends, since not all are of equal value (cf. 9.10; 12.8–9; 19.13–17; 22.19–26; 27.16–21; 37.1–6). Both wisdom literature (see, e.g., Prov 17.17; 18.24; 27.6,10) and Hellenistic writers (e.g., the gnomic poet Theognis, 575; 643–44; 697–98) deal with the topic. 15: Balance their worth, a reference to scales used to determine value.


6.18–37: Discipline and Wisdom. Acquisition of Wisdom means submitting to her harsh discipline, but the rewards are transformative. 18: My child, each section (see vv. 23,32) begins with this address. See 2.1n. When you have gray hair, the search for wisdom is a lifelong process. 19: Eat of her produce, cf. 24.19–22. 21: Like a heavy stone contrasts with toil but little (v. 19). 22: Wisdom is like her name, a play on Heb “musar” (“discipline”) and possibly “sur” (“turn away”). 23–31: Wisdom's discipline, conveyed with images of fetters and bonds, is transformed for the one who submits to it. 26: All your soul and all your might, see Deut 6.5. 30: Purple cord, a reminder of God's commandments (Num 15.38–40). 31: Collar … yoke, for the heavy labor of farm animals; cf. Mt 11.28–30. Glorious robe and splendid crown evoke priestly garments; see 45.7,12; 50.11. 32–37: The student should seek out and listen to the company of elders and meditate (see Ps 1.2) on God's commandments, two primary sources of wisdom for Ben Sira.


7.1–17: Miscellaneous advice. Negative admonitions (“Do not …”), see 4.20–31n. 4–7: Although a wise person might sit in the seat of honor or serve as a judge, ambition is tempered by the potential for disgrace. 9: See 5.6–7. Offering refers to a sacrifice. 15: Farm work, perhaps an allusion to Gen 2.15. For a different view of work and the sage, see 39.24–34. 17: Fire and worms, the Hebrew has only worms. Cf. Isa 66.24.


7.18–36: Social relations. Ben Sira's students are or will be heads of households who must manage a range of social relationships and responsibilities. 18: Ophir, southern Arabia, was famous for gold (1 Kings 9.28; 10.11; Job 22.24; 28.16; Ps 45.9; Isa 13.12). 19: Dismiss a … wife (see v. 26), Deut 24.1–4. 23: Discipline, or “instruct”; see 6.22n. 21: Freedom, see Ex 21.2; Lev 25.39–46; Deut 15.12. 24–25: Daughters, cf. 22.3–6n.; 42.9–13. 27–28: Father … mother, see 3.1–16n. 29–31: Wisdom literature rarely mentions priests and ritual obligations, but they are an important concern in Sirach (35.1–13; 45.6–25; 50.1–21). 29–30: With all your soul … with all your might, Deut 6.5. 31: Portion, Ex 29.27; Lev 7.31–34; Num 18.8–20; Deut 18.3–4. 32: Poor, Deut 15.7–11. 33: Dead, cf. 38.16–23. 36: The end of your life, see 1.13n.


8.1–19: Circumstances to avoid. A series of negative admonitions, as in 4.20–31; 7.1–21; 9.1–9, that highlight Ben Sira's ethics of caution. 1–2: Advice about the powerful and the rich reflects Ben Sira's precarious socioeconomic position. As a scribe, he serves the wealthy classes who thus have power over him. Gold … has perverted the minds of kings, cf. 10.8; Deut 17.14–20. 4: Your ancestors may be insulted for having a senseless descendant. 8–9: The sage serves in the employ of princes and other nobles. Thus the necessity of learning from the sages and the aged, who know the tradition and have experience. 11: Bring you to your feet, an image for an emotional reaction, where one might not guard speech and fall prey to the ambush of the insolent. 12–13: Surety, to offer property as collateral to secure the loan of another. See Prov 6.1–5; 11.15; 17.18; 22.26–27; 4QInstruction. Ben Sira does not forbid giving surety, but he advises extra caution (29.1–7,14–20). 18: The Hebrew plays on the words stranger (“zar”) and secret (“raz”).


9.1–9: Relations with women. More cautionary advice, here about women who might bring shame on the sage. 3: Loose, lit., “strange” or “foreign” (Heb “zarah”); see Prov 5.1–6; 7.4–27. 4: Singing girl, perhaps a prostitute; cf. Isa 23.15–16. 5: Penalties, on seducing a virgin, see Ex 22.16–17. 9: The penalty for adultery with another man's wife was death (Lev 20.10; Deut 22.22).


9.10–16: Making associations. 11–12: In Ben Sira's worldview, sinners might appear to have success, but God will hold them accountable. 13: Probably kings and rulers are meant. Battlements, high on the city walls where one is vulnerable to attack. 15–16: Proper associations should focus on the law of the Most High and fear of the Lord.


9.17–10.5: Wise rulers. A common topic in wisdom literature (Prov 25.4–5; 28.3,16; 29.4,12,14). 10.4–5: Cf. Dan 2.21.


10.6–18: Avoid arrogance and pride. 6–11: Arrogance is foolish in the face of human mortality. 9–11: Ben Sira's emphasis on rulers and nations may reflect the political conditions of his time, particularly the competition between the Ptolemaic and the Seleucid kings (see also vv. 14–17). 9: Dust and ashes, Gen 18.27; Job 30.19; 42.6. 12–18: Pride and sin go hand in hand. 14–15: The verbs overthrows, plucks up, destroys, and plants are reminiscent of Jer 1.10; see also Lk 1.52. 17: Removes … destroys; cf. Job 12.23; erases the memory of them, cf. Eccl 1.11.


10.19–11.6: Honor and humility. True honor accrues to those who fear the Lord (cf. Prov 1.7n) and keep the commandments. 19: Human offspring, the riddle gives the same answer to opposite questions. 24: Fear of the Lord trumps social status. 26–31: Although Ben Sira does not condemn wealth, the correlation of humility and honor reduces the social disparity between wealth and poverty. 11.3: For other comparisons between animal and human behaviors, see Prov 6.6–8; 30.15–19,24–31.


11.7–28: Deliberation and true wealth. Material security does not necessarily signal God's favor. 7–9: See 5.11–12. 14: Cf. Isa 45.6–7; Job 2.10. 17: His favor brings lasting success introduces a moral tension, since sinners often prosper; see v. 21. 21: The devout must trust that God will set things right. 28: One's deeds are reflected in the manner of one's death.


11.29–12.18: Caution in associations. These admonitions exemplify an ethic of caution. 33: Ruin your reputation reflects Ben Sira's concern for a good name (6.1; 15.6; 37.26; 39.10–11; 40.19; 41.11–13; 44.3,8,14). 12.1–7: Give alms to the devout only, because the ungodly will use them against the giver and God hates sinners. 11: One who polishes, that is, in order to be able to see the enemy clearly. Ancient mirrors were highly polished metal. 18: Shake … clap, gestures of derision.


13.1–24: Association with the rich. The sage must associate with the rich, and Ben Sira uses their treatment of the poor as a warning to his students about potential dangers. 2: Clay pot … iron kettle illustrate the difference in social status and the vulnerability of the sage; see vv. 15–20. 7: See 12.18. 8–9: See 31.12–18; Prov 23.1–3; Instruction of Amenemope 23. 13: Caution is the watchword, since any misstep can result in one's downfall. 15–20: Both the sinner and the rich are like predators, the devout and poor like prey, but see v. 24. 21–23: The rich often receive preferential treatment. Cf. Prov 14.20; 19.4.


13.25–14.2: Happiness. 26: A cheerful face reflects the inner condition of the heart, the seat of emotion and thought in ancient understanding.


14.3–19: Use of wealth. 3–10: The miser has the wrong approach to wealth. He is mean to himself and thus cannot see to help others (cf. Prov 11.24–26). 11–19: A contrast with the miser. The proper attitude is to enjoy your share of desired goods but also to present worthy offerings and do good to friends. 12: Hades, in Hebrew Sheol, the abode of the dead. 14: Eccl 8.15; 9.7. 17: Like a garment, Isa 50.9; Ps 102.26. You must die, Gen 2.17; 3.3. 18: Cf. Eccl 1.4; Iliad 6.146–49.


14.20–15.10. The benefits of wisdom. Whoever pursues Wisdom will receive benefits from her. 20: Happy is, a beatitude or macarism (cf., e.g., Ps 1.1; Prov 3.13; Mt 5.3–11; Lk 6.20–23; 4QBeatitudes). 22–25: Cf. Prov 8.32–35. The metaphors of hunter, lover (cf. Song 2.9), and neighbor emphasize single-minded pursuit. 26: On Wisdom as a tree, see 1.20n.; 24.13–17; Prov 3.18. 15.1: On wisdom, law, fears the Lord see 1.11–30n.; 6.32–37; 24.23. 2–3: Wisdom nurtures as a mother and loves as a young bride (cf. Prov 7.4; Wis 7.12; 8.2). Bread and water, cf. 1.16; 24.19–21; Prov 9.1–5. 6: Gladness and a crown of rejoicing, 1.11; 6.31. Everlasting name, immortality through a good reputation.


15.11–16.23: Free will and God's justice. God created humans with the capacity to choose, and so they are responsible for their sins, both individually and corporately. 11–13: Even though God created all things (see 11.14), God cannot do what he hates. 14–17: Humans have had free choice since the beginning, a likely interpretation of Gen 3. 14: Free choice (Heb “yetser”) can have both positive (Isa 26.3; 1 Chr 29.18) and negative (Gen 6.5; 8.1) connotations in the Hebrew Bible. In later Jewish texts, the idea develops that every person possesses a good and an evil “yetser.” 17: Life and death, Deut 30.15. 16.1–4: Having many children was seen as a good (Ps 127.3–5), and one's progeny could protect one's name and reputation (30.1–6). Children also can bring shame (cf. 22.3; 30.12–13). Thus, to die childless is preferable to having a thousand who are ungodly. 7–11: Since God punished the ancient giants (Gen 6.1–4; 1 En. 7; 10), the neighbors of Lot (Gen 18.16–19.29), the doomed nation of the Canaanites (Lev 18.3,25), and the six hundred thousand foot soldiers in the desert (Ex 12.37; Num 14.38), why would God overlook any single stiff-necked person? 12: According to his or her deeds, Ezek 18; Ps 62.12. 17–23: The fictitious speaker, a senseless and misguided person, argues that individuals are hidden from God in the vastness of the cosmos (cf. Job 22.13; Ezek 8.12). The unspoken answer is that God sees everything (23.19–20; 39.20) and judges.


16.24–17.24: Creation and repentance. A meditation on creation that moves from creation to the giving of the law to Israel, and individuals and repentance. 16.26–17.7: An interpretation of Gen 1–3. 26: From the beginning, Gen 1.1; Prov 8.22–23. Boundaries, Job 38.8–11; Pss 104.5–9; 148.5–6. 27–28: Creation is orderly and obeys God (see 33.14–15; 42.15–43.33), but contrast 1 En. 21. 29: Good things, Gen 1.4,10,12, etc. 30: Return, Gen 3.19; Ps 104.29. 17.1: Out of earth, Gen 2.7; 3.19. 2: Authority, v. 4; Gen 1.28; 9.2. 3. His own image, Gen 1.26. 6–7: Knowledge … good and evil, in Genesis these things come to humans as a result of disobedience (Gen 2.4–3.24). Ben Sira ignores that part of the story. 11–14: A shift to Israel and the giving of the Torah. 11: Law of life, the Torah; see 45.5; Deut 30.15–20. 12–13: Glorious majesty … voice, a reference to the Sinai theophany and covenant (Ex 19). 14: Neighbor, Lev 19.18 (cf. Ex 20.13–17; Deut 5.17–21). 15–24: God sees human sin (cf. 15.19) and judges, but almsgiving and repentance allow a return. 17. The Lord's own portion, Deut 32.8–9. 22: Signet ring (Jer 22.24; Hag 2.23) and apple of his eye (Deut 32.10) suggest a special relationship with God.


17.25–32: Mercy and repentance. God's mercy allows repentance. 27–28: The dead in Hades (see 14.12n) cannot praise God (cf., e.g., Pss 6.5; 30.9; 88.10–12; Bar 2.17), which should be humanity's response to God (39.12–35; 43.11,27–33). 30–31: If the sun's light can fail, how much more can flesh and blood. 32: Dust and ashes, see 10.9n.


18.1–14: God's majesty and compassion. Human frailty and mortality prompt God's compassion. 4–7: Cf. 43.27–33. 4: To none, cf. 42.17. 7: Have finished, trying “to fathom the wonders of the Lord” (v. 6). 8: What are human beings, Ps 8.4. 9: Number of days, Ps 90.10. 11: Cf. Ps 103.14. 13: Shepherd, cf. Ps 23.1–4; Isa 40.11; Ezek 34.11–16.


18.15–29: Speech and action. A gracious person speaks kind words and the wise person is cautious in everything. 18: The fool is a frequent foil to the wise person in wisdom literature. 21: Falling ill is related to sin (cf. 38.9–15). 23: Test, cf. Ex 17.2; Deut 6.16. 24: Consideration of the day of death should affect how one acts in life.


18.30–19.17: Self-control and gossip. 31: Laughingstock, that is, exposed to public shame (cf. 6.4; 13.7; 42.11). 19.2: Cf. Prov 31.2–5. 3: Snatched away, will die an untimely death. 10: Let it die with you, self-control means not repeating gossip. 13–17: Do not believe everything you hear (v. 15) but first ask neighbor or friend directly. 17: Law of the Most High, cf. Lev 19.17–18.


19.20–30: Wisdom contrasted with cleverness. 20: Wisdom … fear of the Lord … fulfillment of the law, the basic triad in Sirach; see 1.11–30n. 23: Cleverness (Gk “panourgia”) has a negative connotation, since it is deceitful. 29–30: A person's outward appearance reflects his or her inner nature; cf. 13.25–26.


20.1–31: Topics related to speech. The advice in this section appeals to avoidance of shame. A significant difference between proper and improper speech concerns speaking at the proper time. 4: Sinners cannot be compelled to act properly any more than a eunuch can engage in sexual intercourse. 5–6: Cf. Prov 17.27–28. 9–12: Although the sages argued for moral laws of cause-and-effect, they recognized both ironies and paradoxes; cf. Prov 14.12; 16.25; Eccl 9.1–12. 20: Cf. Prov 26.7. 24–26: On lying, see 7.13; 25.2; Prov 6.17; 12.22; Ps 5.6.


21.1–10: Sin and repentance. Sin can inflict grievous, even mortal, wounds, but forgiveness is possible. 3: Lawlessness, equated with sin, emphasizes the importance of fulfilling the law. 5: Prayer of the poor, cf. 35.17–22a; Deut 15.9. 9: Bundle of tow, highly combustible flax. Fire, punishment in this lifetime rather than after death. 10: Hades, see 14.12n.


21.11–22.18: The wise and the foolish. 12: Clever, here in a positive sense (cf. 19.23). 13–14: Increase like a flood … broken jar, the knowledge of the wise overflows, while the fool's mind can hold nothing (cf. 22.9). 19: Compare the same imagery used positively of Wisdom in 6.24–25,29–30. 22–24: Being educated means having good manners. 22.1: Filthy stone, a rock used for wiping after a bowel movement. 3–6: Son … daughter, sons were valued more highly than daughters in Ben Sira's social world (cf. 7.24–25; 42.9–14), but both can bring shame on their father. 6: Thrashing, corporal punishment was the norm in parenting and education (30.12–13; Prov 13.24; 23.13–14). 9: See 21.13–14. 11: For the dead nothing more exists; for the fool the rest of life is at stake. 12: Seven days, the traditional mourning period, but cf. 38.17. 13: Spattered, the image is of an animal shaking off that affects anyone standing close by. 16–18: Fool's resolve contrasts with the resolve of the wise.


22.19–26: Preserving friendship. See also 6.5–17. Even true and loyal friends might make mistakes that require reconciliation. True friends stand by friends in good and bad times. 25–26: Shelter a friend runs counter to Ben Sira's usual ethic of caution; cf. 11.29.


22.27–23.6. Prayer for self-control. 23.2–3: Whips … discipline, an appeal to the idea that corporal punishment will prevent mistakes, in this case sins. 23.1,4: O Lord, Father, cf. 51.10.


23.7–15: Self-control in speech. This poem connects with the theme of the previous section. 9: On misuse of God's name, see Ex 20.7; Deut 5.11. On oaths, Lev 5.4; Num 3.1–16. 12: Death, perhaps a reference to blasphemy (Lev 24.16). Inheritance of Jacob, the Israelites. 14: Curse the day of your birth, see Job 3.3–5; Jer 20.14–18.


23.16–27. Sexual sins. A poem on sexual license of both men and women. 16: Two kinds … third, a numerical proverb, often used in wisdom literature (cf. 25.1–2,7; 26.5–6,28; 50.25–26; Prov 30.18–19,21–23). 21: Death was the stipulated punishment for adultery (Lev 20.10; Deut 22.22–24). Here the punishment is public but not specified (see also v. 24). 19: Eyes of the Lord, God knows all human actions (cf. 16.17–22). 23: Disobeyed the law, Ex 20.14; Lev 20.10; Deut 5.18; 22.22. 25–26: The adulteress's children will not flourish (cf. Wis 3.16–19; 4.3–6; also Deut 5.9–10). 27: The reference to fear of the Lord and the commandments leads directly to Wisdom's self-praise in ch 24.


24.1–22. Wisdom's self-praise. An aretalogy (first-person praise of oneself, often connected with the Egyptian goddess Isis) in which Wisdom is personified as a woman (Prov 8.22–36; cf. Bar 3.9–4.4; Wis 7.22–8.1) and dwells in the Jerusalem Temple. 1–2: Her people, Israel; the assembly of the Most High, the heavenly host or divine council (cf. Ps 82.1,6–7). 3: From the mouth of the Most High evokes Gen 1. Covered like a mist, cf. Gen 1.2; Wis 7.25. 4: Pillar of cloud, see Ex 13.21–22; 33.9–10; Wis 10.17–18. 6: Wisdom has a universal reach (cf. 1.15). 7: Resting place, Job 28.23; 1 En. 42. 8–12: Wisdom, who was created in the beginning (cf. Gen 1.1), dwells with Israel (cf. Bar 3.36–37) in the Jerusalem Temple. 9: Prov 8.22–23. 10: Holy tent, an allusion to the tabernacle (Ex 25.8–9), which represents the Temple. Ministered, Wisdom functions liturgically as a priest. 12: Portion of the Lord, cf. 17.17. 13–17: A comparison of Wisdom with plants, perfume, and fragrant substances, emphasizing her beauty and expanse and her connection with the Temple. See 50.8–12 where roses, cedar, palm, cypress, and olive describe the high priest Simon II. 13: Lebanon, a mountain range in modern Lebanon and Syria famous for its forests. Hermon, a mountain on the border of modern Israel and Syria. 14: En-gedi and Jericho, oases in the region near the Dead Sea. 15: These ingredients were used in the service of the Temple (Ex 30.22–38), which is infused with Wisdom's presence, just as with incense. 19–22: Wisdom is better than fine food and drink, and those who eat and drink will desire more (cf. 6.19; Prov 9.1–6). 23: Ben Sira is the first to relate Torah and wisdom in this way; see also Bar 4.1.


24.24–34: Ben Sira's interpretation. 23: The book of the covenant of the Most High God (cf. Ex 24.7; Deut 33.4) embodies the eternal, timeless Wisdom of vv. 3–22 (cf. Deut 4.5–8), an important statement about the confluence of the Torah and the wisdom traditions. 25–27: The Pishon, Tigris, Euphrates, and Gihon flow from the Garden of Eden (Gen 2.10–14). 28–29: Wisdom will never be fully grasped, not from the first man to the last one; cf. 1.4–8. 30–34: Ben Sira connects his own teaching to both Torah and Wisdom through the metaphor of a canal, water channel, river, and sea. 33: Pour out teaching like prophecy, Ben Sira's teaching has a revelatory quality to it.


25.1–11: Praiseworthy things. 1–2,7: For other numerical proverbs in Sirach, see 23.16; 26.5–6,28; 50.25–26. 3–6: The value of wisdom in older people. 6: Cf. 1.11,18 where crown is associated with fear of the Lord and wisdom. 8: The Torah prohibits plowing with ox and ass together (Deut 22.10). Here it refers to an unequal marriage of some sort—perhaps a wise man with a foolish wife or in a polygamous marriage with incompatible wives (cf. 26.6; 37.11). To serve an inferior would bring shame.


25.13–26.27: Evil and good wives. A meditation on the qualities of good and bad wives. Ben Sira's overall negativity about women derives primarily from the ways that they can bring shame upon a husband or father. Even so, his negative language about women exceeds that found in other contemporary texts. 16: Cf. Prov 21.19; 25.24; 27.15. 19: A strong condemnation given Ben Sira's statements about sinners elsewhere (cf. 5.6; 12.6). 22: Disgrace, the implication is that the man cannot control the critical facets of his life, leading to shame. A wife's economic achievements are praised in Prov 31.10–31. 24: Placing blame on the woman became the traditional interpretation of Gen 3 (cf. 2 Cor 11.3; 1 Tim 2.14), even though Ben Sira goes beyond Genesis in his blaming Eve. Because of her we all die, cf., however, 17.1–2 where human beings have a fixed life span from the start. 26: Separate, see Deut 24.1–4 for the reasons a man can divorce his wife. 26.1–4: Ben Sira emphasizes the benefits to the husband of having a good wife. 5–12: The warning about a bad wife leads to the problems of a headstrong daughter. 5: On numerical proverbs, see 23.16n. 6: Jealous of a rival, likely enmity among polygamous wives (cf. 37.11). 12: Tent peg … quiver … arrow, transparent metaphors for indiscriminate sexuality. 13–18: While the good wife has virtues, her face, legs, and feet are compared with the holy lampstand (the menorah in the Temple) and golden pillars (probably columns in the Temple), unlike the bad wife and daughter whose bodies are emphasized (vv. 25.17,21; 26.9,11,12). 19–27: Although not in the Hebrew, the Greek and Syriac translations contain these verses, and they were likely part of Ben Sira's book. 20–21: The concern is for legitimacy of one's offspring, who then prosper (cf. 23.22–26). 20: Seek a fertile field, an agricultural metaphor that focuses on the woman's childbearing capacity (cf. Prov 5.15–18). 25: Headstrong, see 26.10.


26.28–27.15: Integrity and speech. 28: For numerical proverbs, see 23.16n. Warrior, perhaps a mistake of the Greek translator. No Hebrew survives for this verse but the Syriac has “noble man.” 26.29–27.2: These verses do not condemn business, although business can involve corruption (cf. Prov 11.1; 20.10). 8: Glorious robe, see 6.31n.; cf. Job 29.14. 12: The topic of proper associations and their impact on a person is common in wisdom literature, cf. 13.1; 37.12; Prov 20.19; 22.24–25; 23.20–21; Letter of Aristeas 130.


27.16–29: Relationships with companions. 16–21: Keeping a secret is a mark of true friendship (cf. 8.17–19; 22.22; Prov 25.9–10). 22: Winks, a sign of duplicity (cf. Prov 6.12–14; 10.10; 16.30). 24: The Lord hates him, cf. 12.6. 26–27: That the wicked are caught in the traps they set is a common idea in wisdom literature and the psalms (e.g., Prov 26.27; Eccl 10.8–9; Pss 7.15; 9.15–16; 35.7-8; 141.10). 29: Pain at death is a sign of God's judgment.


27.30–28.7: Forgiveness. 28.1: By keeping a strict account of their sins, God's judgment is just. 2: Forgive … your sins will be pardoned, in Sirach pious acts, such as honoring parents (3.3,14) almsgiving (3.30), and forgiveness, count against one's sins. 6–7: Recalling death, the commandments, and the covenant should temper hard feelings. Ben Sira often appeals to death as motivation for proper behavior (7.36; 14.12; 18.24; 38.20).


28.8–26: Destructive speech. 8–12: Strife or social disharmony is a concern in small communities and is a common topic in wisdom literature; see Prov 6.14,19; 10.12; 16.18; etc. 10: Here wealth connects with wrath; cf. 13.24 where riches are positively valued if free from sin. 13: Double-tongued, see 5.14n. 14–15: Slander, lit., “third tongue,” since slander is not directed to the person being slandered. Thus the slanderer is the third tongue 19–20: Yoke … fetters, see 6.24–30 where Wisdom employs these devices. 21: Hades, see 14.12n. 24: Fence in, with a hedge of thorn bushes.


29.1–20: Loans, alms, and surety. 1–7: Biblical law regulates lending and taking of interest, which could not be exacted from Israelites (Ex 22.25; Lev 25.36–37; Deut 15.7–11; 23.19–20; 24.10–13). Ben Sira's warnings about possible default on loans reflect his ethic of caution (cf. 8.12–13). 8–13: In addition to storing up treasure (cf. Mt 6.19–20), giving alms atones for sins (3.30), brings God's favor (17.22), works like sacrifice (35.4), and rescues from trouble (40.24). 9: The commandment, Deut 15.7–8. 14–20: Surety, see 8.12–13n.


29.21–28: Depending on others. Exceeding one's resources results in dependence that brings shame. 21: See 39.26. 22: The poor have something but often live on the verge of destitution. See 40.28n. 25–26: As a guest one might be treated more like a servant.


30.1–13: Raising sons. A son properly raised reflects positively on his father and enhances his honor and reputation. 1–6: Severe discipline for parenting children was usual in antiquity (cf. Prov 13.24; 22.15; 23.13–14; 29.15). 4: On a son as the image of his father, see Gen 5.3; Tob 9.6. 6: Avenger, the son will complete his father's business and settle scores. 7–13: Spoiling and pampering are the opposite of discipline. 12: Stubborn, cf. Deut 21.18–21.


30.14–25: Health and food. 17: Death is better, cf. 16.3; Job 3.11–17; Tob 3.6. 18–20: Offerings of food to the dead, making a sacrifice to an idol, and a eunuch trying to engage in sex are metaphors for uselessness. 23: Indulge yourself, Eccl 5.18–20; 8.15; 9.7–10.


31.1–11: Wealth. 1: Wakefulness, cf. 42.9 concerning daughters. 7: Cf. Eccl 5.10. 8–11: In light of v. 5, the rhetorical questions suggest that those not corrupted by money are few. 10: Tested, see 2.4–6n.


31.12–32.13. Table manners. Ben Sira's students needed to learn proper manners in order to navigate social occasions. The table of the great, or banquet, was an event where one could garner acclaim and honor or experience embarrassment and shame. Advice about manners is frequent in Egyptian wisdom texts, such as Ptahhotep and Amenemope. 12–18: Proper table manners (cf. Prov 23.1–3). 19–24: Moderation leads to good health. 25–31: On wine drinking and its deleterious effects, see Prov 20.1; 23.29–35; 31.4–5. The background may be the symposium, which featured much eating, drinking, and entertainment. See Philo, On the Contemplative Life 48–63; Letter of Aristeas 187–300. 32.1: The master of the feast was responsible for the needs of those attending (2 Macc 2.27; Letter of Aristeas 182). 7–9: The young were expected to keep silence before elders; cf. Job 29.8; 32.4,6.


32.14–33.6: Deliberate judgments. 14: Rise early, for prayer (see 39.5). 16–17: True judgments, perhaps a reference to the sage in an official capacity (cf. 38.31–33). According to his liking, the sinner contrasts with those who fear the Lord. 33.1: No evil will befall reflects Ben Sira's view that God will protect and rescue the faithful. 3: Divine oracle, likely the Urim and Thummin (45.10; Ex 28.30; Lev 8.8; Num 27.21; 1 Sam 14.41–42).


33.7–15: The pairs. God created the cosmos in pairs (v. 15), an order that can be observed and extends to humans, as the wise and foolish or the godly and the sinner (v. 14). 7–9: Sabbath and liturgical festivals (cf. Gen 1.14; 2.3). 10: Gen 2.7; 3.19. 12: Blessed and exalted, figures such as Abraham and Moses. Brought near to himself, a likely reference to the priesthood. Some he cursed, perhaps referring to the Canaanites (cf. 16.9). 13: Clay, cf. Isa 29.16; 45.9; 64.8; Jer 18.6.


33.16–19: Ben Sira the sage. For other authorial self-references, see 24.30–34; 34.9–13; 39.12–13; 50.27. 16: Keep vigil, a prophetic image; see Ezek 33.7; Hab 2.1 (cf. Jer 1.12; 31.28; 44.27 for the same verb). A gleaner collects what remains after the harvest; see Deut 24.19–22. 19: Cf. 24.34.


33.20–33: The household. 20–24: Loss of control over property and family brought a stain upon your honor. 25–33: Slavery (cf. 7.20–21) was a sanctioned institution, which was regulated in Israelite law (Ex 21.2–11,20–21,26–27; Lev 25.39–46; Deut 15.12–18). 31: Bought him with blood, the high cost of purchasing a slave justified good treatment. 32: Runs away, cf. Deut 23.15–16.


34.1–8: Dreams. Dreams, divinations, and omens do not provide reliable knowledge. Ben Sira sets these against the law and wisdom (v. 8). He may be opposing the apocalyptic movement, which emphasized knowledge through dreams and visions. 2: Pursues the wind, cf. Eccl 1.14. 3: Dreams are a projection of the dreamer, a view that seems very modern. 4: Clean … unclean, cf. Job 14.4. 6: From the Most High, only divinely inspired dreams are acceptable (cf. Gen 28.10–16; 37.5–10; Judg 7.13–15).


34.9–13: Experience through travel. See 39.4; 51.13.


34.14–20: Fear of the Lord. See 1.11–30; 2.1–18. 14: Spirit … will live, in the sense of being energized, encouraged, not in a postmortem existence. 19: Common images in Israel's hymnic tradition (e.g., Pss 3.3; 7.10; 18.2,17,35; 61.3–4; 91.1–4; 121.3–6).


34.21–35.26. Sacrifice and true worship. Ben Sira supported the Temple and its priesthood (cf. 50.1–24) and advocated sacrificing according to the law. Social justice and ethical behavior must motivate and accompany sacrifice, however. 21: Blemished, cf. Lev 22.18–25. 24–27: Ben Sira connects material resources with the ability to live (cf. 29.15; 31.4). Thus, taking what little the poor have constitutes murder. 30: Touching a corpse makes one ritually impure, which is alleviated through washing (Num 19.10–20). 31: Fasts, perhaps a reference to the Day of Atonement (Lev 23.27–32).


35.1–13: Keeping the law, heeding the commandments, giving alms all atone for sin like sacrifice; cf. 3.3,14,30. God looks favorably on sacrifices made willingly and generously. 2: Offering of well-being, cf. Leviticus 3. 3: Choice flour, cf. Leviticus 2. 4: Thank offering, cf. Lev 7.12–21. 6: Empty-handed, see Ex 23.15; Deut 16.16. 10: First fruits, see Ex 23.16,19; 34.22,26; Lev 2.14; 23.10,17. 11: Tithe, one-tenth of one's produce and harvest, dedicated to God (cf. Deut 14.22–29).


35.14–26: Ben Sira's claim that God is just leads to an indictment of unrighteous individuals generally and the nations specifically, which forms the transition to the prayer of 36.1–22. Ben Sira may be alluding to the political situation of his time. 17: On divine concern for the vulnerable orphan and widow, see, e.g., Deut 10.17–18; Ps 68.5.


36.1–22: Prayer for the deliverance of Israel. A prayer of lament for deliverance from foreign nations, perhaps a reference to Seleucid rulers. 4–7: A series of allusions to the Exodus. 4: The events of the Exodus convinced the Egyptians that God is the Lord; see Ex 7.17; 8.22; 14.4. 6: Signs … wonders … hand … right arm, see Ex 7.3; 11.9–10; 15.6; Deut 4.34; 7.19. 10: The Hebrew words day (Heb “qets”) and appointed time (Heb “moʿed”) occur frequently in Jewish eschatological literature. 13: A widespread prophetic hope that God would gather the dispersed of Israel (cf. Isa 49.5; 56.8; Jer 23.7–8; 32.36–37; Mic 2.12). 17: Called by your name, see Deut 28.10; Jer 14.9. Firstborn, Ex 4.22. 18: Your dwelling, God's presence was thought to reside in the Temple; see 1 Kings 8.12; Ps 132.14. 20–21: Fulfill the prophecies reflects a developing view of prophecy in this period as prediction of future events (cf. 1QpHab 7.1–5).


36.23–37.15: Choosing wives, friends, and counselors. 26: One girl is preferable, that is, as the man's choice of a wife. 29: A helper fit for him, see Gen 2.18. 30: A fugitive and a wanderer, like Cain (Gen 4.12,14). 37.1–6: On friends, see 6.15–17; 9.10–16; 19.13–17; 22.19–26; 27.16–21. 3: Inclination to evil, Heb “yetser”; see 15.14n. 11: Her rival, perhaps another wife (26.6).


37.16–31: Deliberative speech and moderation. 17–18: Cf. 5.13. 26: The themes of achieving honor and having immortality through one's name run through Sirach (e.g., 10.28–31; 15.6; 33.23; 39.9–11; 40.19; 41.11–13). 27–31: Cf. 31.12–31.


38.1–15: Illness and physicians. While Ben Sira recommends treatment by a physician, he reaffirms the traditional idea that illness results from sin. 5: Water made sweet, see Ex 15.23–25. 9–15: On sin as a cause of illness, see 18.19–21; Deut 28.21–22,27,35; Jn 9.2; and Job 10; 33–34 on the relationship between sin and suffering. 11: On generosity in sacrifice, see 35.10–11.


38.16–23: Mourning. 16: Do not neglect the burial, proper burial was a religious obligation (cf. Tob 1.17–18; 4.3–4; 6.15; 12.12; 14.12–13). 17: One day, or two, a much shorter period than stipulated in 22.12.


38.24–39.11: The trades and the scribe. Ancient scribes/sages like Ben Sira were intellectuals and public figures, not only producers of documents. The contrast between the sage and artisans, farmers, and tradespersons was popular in Egyptian wisdom, such as the Satire of the Trades (the Instruction of Kheti), but Ben Sira has a more positive attitude toward these occupations than the Egyptian text. 24: Leisure, artisans and tradespersons are too busy to take the time for study. 27: Signets of seals were used to make impressions that authorized identity, much as a personal signature functions today. 32–34: Artisans, farmers, and tradespersons maintain the fabric of the world, but the scribe enables society to function. 39.4: Cf. 34.12–13. 6: Filled with the spirit of understanding, the scribe's wisdom comes through study (38.34c–39.3) and revelatory inspiration. 9–11: The wise scribe will live on through his memory and name; cf. 37.26; 44.10–15.


39.12–35: Praise of God's creation. A hymn of praise (vv. 16–31) with an introduction (vv. 12–15) and a personal conclusion (32–35). 12: Like the full moon, Ben Sira's teaching illuminates (cf. 24.32). 13–14: Reminiscent of Wisdom in 24.13–17. 16: Very good, cf. Gen 1.4,10,12,18,21,25,31. Appointed time, see 36.10; 39.34; 48.10; Eccl 3.11. 17: The waters stood in a heap (cf. Ex 15.8; Josh 3.16). At the word of his mouth, cf. Gen 1.9–10; Ps 33.6. 23: Watered land into salt, Sodom and Gomorrah (cf. Gen 19.24–26). 25–27: Though the good share the good things of creation, sinners have both good things and bad. Yet the good things in creation turn to evils for sinners. 28–31: Elements created to punish the wicked. 29: Created for vengeance, cf. Job 38.23.


40.1–27: Life's miseries and joys. An explication of Ben Sira's views expressed in 39.22–31 about the righteous and unrighteous. 1: Yoke, a positive and negative image in Sirach; cf. 6.23–31; 26.7; 28.19–20; 30.13; 33.27; 51.26. Adam, see Gen 3.17–19. Mother of all the living, see Job 1.21; Gen 3.20 (where the phrase refers to Eve). 8–11: In order for Ben Sira to maintain the idea that God punishes sinners especially, sinners must suffer seven times more (cf. 39.28–31). 10: Flood, see Gen 6–8. 11: See Gen 2.7; 3.19; 6.3; also Eccl 12.7. Ben Sira apparently distinguishes between the material dust from which humans were created and the divine breath by which they were animated. 15: See 23.25; Wis 3.16–19; 4.3–6. 17: On the benefits of almsgiving, see 3.30; 12.3; 17.22; 29.12; 35.4; 40.24. 18–27: A series of “better than” proverbs of the form “x and y are good, but z is better.” 26–27: Fear of the Lord exceeds everything; cf., for example, 1.11–20. 27: Garden of blessing, see Gen 2.10,15.


40.28–41.13: Death and reputation. 28: Better to die than to beg, destitution differs from being poor and represents a form of social death (cf. Lk 16.3). 41.3–4: Death's decree … for all, see 14.12,17; Gen 3.19. Hades, see 14.12n. 5–10: The main thought concerns disgrace or shame. The sins of the parents devolve to their children; see Deut 5.9; Wis 3.16–19; 4.3–6. See 3.1–16 on parents and children. 8: Woe, a prophetic form. 10: See 40.11n. 11: Virtuous name, see 37.26; 39.9,11; Prov 22.1; Eccl 7.1.


41.14–42.8: Appropriate and inappropriate shame. The most extensive teaching on shame in Sirach (cf. 4.20–28), here differentiating between things that bring inappropriate shame and things of which to be appropriately ashamed. 14–16: An introduction summarizing the theme. 17–18: Be ashamed … before, shows the public nature of honor and shame. 42.1: Find favor, the end result of proper shame is honor. 2: The law and the covenant head the list of things not to be ashamed of. Even the ungodly deserve justice. 4–5: On merchants, see 26.29–27.2; on corporal punishment for children and slaves, see 7.23; 30.1–2; 33.25–30. 8: Approved by all echoes 42.1.


42.9–14: Daughters. As in other passages on women (cf. 22.3–6; 23.22–27; 25.13–26.27), Ben Sira worries about how their behavior affects a man's status. 9–10: Virginity and fidelity guaranteed legitimate children and proper inheritance (cf. 23.22–23; cf. Deut 22.13–29.) 11: A man's inability to control important culturally significant aspects of his life, here daughters, brings shame. 13: From a woman, perhaps a reference to Eve (cf. 25.24). 14: The most pernicious articulation of Ben Sira's misogyny (cf. 25.13–26; 36.26–31).


42.15–43.33: The works of God in nature. A hymn of praise beginning with a poem on God's omniscience (42.15–21), followed by an explanation of the wonders of the natural order (42.22–43.26), and ending with praise of God (43.27–33). 15: By the word, cf. Gen 1.1–31; Ps 33.6. 16: Full of his glory, God's creation reveals God's glory; cf. Isa 6.3 17: Holy ones, God's heavenly court or angels (cf. Job 15.15). 18–20: God's knowledge is inscrutable to humans, although they can apprehend some things through divine revelation (cf. 48.25).19: What has been and what is to be, cf. Isa 41.22–23; 44.7; reveals … hidden things, cf. Dan 2.22. 21: Counselor, cf. Isa 40.13. 24: All things come in pairs, cf. 33.14–15. 43.1–12: For other lists of natural phenomena, cf. Job 28.23–28; Ps 104. 7: Festal days, the moon sets the liturgical calendar rather than the sun and moon together as in Gen 1.14, perhaps indicating Ben Sira's rejection of a solar calendar used by some Jews. 8: A word play on new moon (Heb “ḥodesh”) and renews itself (Heb “mitḥadesh”). 14: Storehouses, where weather phenomena are kept; cf. Deut 28.12; Ps 135.7; Jer 10.13; 51.16 (wind); Job 38.22 (snow and hail). 16–17: The images evoke divine theophanies; cf. Ps. 18.7–15. 17: At his will, cf. Ps 148.8. 19: Like salt, cf. Ps 147.16. 23–25: Cf. Job 26.12; Pss 104.24–26; 107.23–24. 27: He is the all, in the sense that creation everywhere displays God's glory. 32: I have seen forms an inclusio with 42.15 to bookend the poem's beginning and end. 33: Connects praise of God in creation to praise of human beings in 44.1–50.24.


44.1–50.24: Praise of Israel's ancestors. A long section in which Ben Sira celebrates significant figures from Israel's past, who were rewarded with a lasting name. He emphasizes covenant along with the offices of prophet, priest, and king, concluding with praise of a contemporary, the high priest Simon II.


44.1–15: Introduction to the praise. 1: Famous men, the Hebrew and Syriac have men of piety. Ben Sira includes no women in his list. 3–7: The varieties of leadership celebrated focus on royal and administrative roles, prophetic and poetic spokespersons, and landed gentry. 8–11: Left behind … no memory, Ben Sira recognizes that some righteous people have perished as though they never existed, which runs counter to the rest of Sirach, but he says that their righteous deeds will be recalled. 12–15: Ben Sira's own praise enacts his promise that their wisdom will be remembered.


44.16–23: The patriarchs. 16: See 49.14. Enoch … was taken up, see Gen 5.24. The phrase example of repentance may show knowledge of nonbiblical traditions about Enoch. 17–18: Noah … perfect and righteous, see Gen 6.9; 7.1. Everlasting covenants, see Gen 9.11–12. 19–21: Abraham … father of a multitude, see Gen 17.4–8. 20: Abraham kept the law, even before Moses gave it (cf. Jubilees 13). Covenant in his flesh, circumcision; see Gen 17.9–14. Tested, the binding of Isaac (Gen 22). 21: Oath, see Gen 12.3; 13.16; 15.5,18; 22.15–18. 22–23: Abraham's covenant passed to Isaac and Jacob (Gen 17.19–21; 28.4,13–15). With his blessings, see Gen 27. Distributed them among the twelve tribes, the sons of Jacob; cf. Gen 49.


44.23–45.26: Later covenantal figures. 45.1–2: Equal in glory, perhaps referring to Moses being like God to Pharaoh (Ex 7.1) or to Moses's shining face (Ex 34.29–35). 3: Miracles, the “plagues” against Egypt; Ex 7.1–11.10; 12.29–32. Commandments, Ex 20.1–17; Deut 5.1–22. Glory, Ex 33.18–23. 4: Meekness, Num 12.3. 5: Dark cloud, Ex 20.21; 24.18. Face to face, Num 12.8. Teach, Deut 4.1,5; 6.1. 6–22: Ben Sira spends more time on Aaron than any other figure, reflecting his interest in priesthood. 6–7: Tribe of Levi, Ex 4.14. Everlasting covenant, Ex 29.9; 40.15. 8–12: On priestly vestments, see Ex 28–29. 10: Urim and Thummim, Ex 28.30. 12: A gold crown is not among the biblical vestments but acknowledges priestly leadership of Israel in Ben Sira's time. 14: The daily cereal offering (Lev 6.19–23). 15: Ordained … anointed, Ex 28.41; Lev 8.1–30. Bless his people, 50.20; Num 6.23–27. 17: Teach, Lev 10.11; Deut 33.10. 18–19: See Num 16. 20–22: First fruits … eat the sacrfices, see Num 18. No portion … inheritance, see Num 18.20; Deut 12.12. 23: Zealous, see Num 25.10–13; 1 Macc 2.26,54. 24: Covenant of friendship, see Num 25.10–12. 26: A benediction likely directed at the contemporary high priest Simon II and his successors.


46.1–20: Joshua, Caleb, the judges, and Samuel. 1: Mighty in war, see Josh 6–11. Successor of Moses, Deut 34.9; Josh 1.5; 3.7. As his name implies, a play on words, since Joshua's name means “The Lord is salvation.” 4: Josh 10.12–14. 5: Hailstones, Josh 10.11. 7: Proved … stilled, Num 14. 8: Two alone, Num 26.65. Six hundred thousand, Ex 12.37; Num 11.21. Land flowing with milk and honey, the phrase describing the bounteous nature of Canaan; see, for example, Num 14.8. 9: Inheritance, Num 14.6–14. 11–12: Only the judges who did not commit idolatry (as Gideon did in Judg 8.22–50) deserve praise. Their bones send forth new life, see 49.10; 2 Kings 13.21. 13–20: Samuel anointed rulers (1 Sam 10.1; 16.3) and acted as judge (1 Sam 7.15), prophet (1 Sam 3.19–20), and priest (1 Sam 7.9). 16–18: 1 Sam 7.7–11. 19: See 1 Sam 12.1–5. 20: Lifted up his voice from the ground, 1 Sam 28.8–19.


47.1–22: Nathan, David, and Solomon. 1: Nathan, 2 Sam 7.2–4; 12.1–15; 1 Chr 17.1–4. 2: Fat, see Lev 4.8,19. 3: Cf. 1 Sam 17.34–37. 4: 1 Sam 17.49–51 (cf. 2 Sam 21.18–19). 6: Tens of thousands, 1 Sam 18.7. 8–10: David is remembered as a composer of psalms, and he organized the Temple service (1 Chr 23–26). 11: Took away his sins, in the Bathsheba affair (2 Sam 11–12). Covenant of kingship, 2 Sam 7.12–16; 23.5; Ps 89.3–4. 13: Build a house, the Temple in Jerusalem (1 Kings 5–8). 16–17: See 1 Kings 4.29–34; 10.1–10. 18–21: Solomon violated the laws of the king (Deut 17.14–20) by amassing great wealth and marrying many women. As a result his kingdom was divided (1 Kings 11.31–39). 22: Root, see Isa 11.10. 23–25: Rehoboam … Jeroboam, 1 Kings 11.43–14.31. 24: Exiled, 2 Kings 17.6–8,18.


48.1–16: Elijah and Elisha. 1–3: 1 Kings 17.1; 18.1–40. 5: Raised a corpse, 1 Kings 17.21–22. 7: Heard rebuke, 1 Kings 19.8–9. 8: Anointed kings … prophets to succeed, 1 Kings 19.15–16,19–21. 9: 2 Kings 2.1–12. 10: It is written, Mal 4.5–6. 12: 2 Kings 2.1–12. 13–14: 2 Kings 13.20–21. 15–16: An interpretation of the cause of the destruction of the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century bce; see 2 Kings 18.11–12.


48.17–25: Hezekiah and Isaiah. 17: 2 Kings 20.20; 2 Chr 32.5–6,30. 18–20: The Assyrian siege of Jerusalem (2 Kings 18–19; Isa 36; 2 Chr 32). 18: Sennacherib, the Assyrian king (705–681 bce). 21: 2 Kings 19.35–37; 2 Chr 32.20–21. 22: 2 Kings 18.3. 23: 2 Kings 20.8–11; Isa 38.7–8. 24: Comforted the mourners, Isa 40.1–2.


49.1–13: Josiah and succeeding ancestors. 2: 2 Kings 23.4–25. 4–7: A summary of the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 bce. As in the Deuteronomistic History, only these three kings were fully righteous. 6: Jeremiah had foretold, Jer 7.12–15. 7: See Jer 1.5,9–10. 8: Ezek 1.4–14; 10. 9: See textual note g and cf. Ezek 14.14,20. 10: Ben Sira knows the Twelve Minor Prophets (Hosea–Malachi) as one book; cf. 46.12. 11–13: Postexilic leaders: Zerubbabel (Ezra 3.2; Hag 2.23), Jeshua (Ezra 3.2; Hag 1.12; Zech 3; 6.9–13), Nehemiah (Nehemiah, esp. 2.17–3.32).


49.14–16: Concluding ancestors. A conclusion that extends back to the first human. 14: Enoch, see 44.16n. 15: Joseph, see Gen 39–50, esp. 50.25–26; Ex 13.19. 16: Shem (Gen 9.18), Seth (Gen 5.3), Enosh (Gen 5.6–11), and Adam (Gen 1.26–31).


50.1–24: The priest Simon II. The son of Onias was high priest from 219 bce to 196 bce. Ben Sira emphasizes his dual roles as ruler and priest through a theme of glory. 1–4: Simon's public works projects; cf. those of Hezekiah (48.17) and Nehemiah (49.13). 5–11: The language recalls that of Wisdom in ch 24 and the heavenly bodies in ch 43. 5: House of the curtain, the Temple. 12–21: A detailed description of the Temple ritual and sacrifices, either for the Day of Atonement (Lev 16) or the daily offering (45.14; Num 28.1–8). 16: Trumpets, see Num 10.10. 20: Blessing of the Lord, see Lev 9.22–23; Num 6.22–27. 22–24: A concluding benediction.


50.25–29: Epilogue. 25–26: Seir (Edom), the Philistines, and Shechem (the Samaritans) were traditional enemies of Israel. 27: The author gives his name, probably Yeshua ben Eleazar ben Sira. Poured forth wisdom, cf. 24.23–34.


51.1–12: A hymn of thanksgiving. This hymn has many linguistic reminiscences of the Psalms. 5,6: Hades, see 14.12n. 10: Father, see 23.1,4. 12: After v. 12, the medieval Hebrew manuscripts insert a hymn based on Ps 136.


51.13–30. Ben Sira's search for Wisdom. An acrostic poem in the first person on the sage's search for Wisdom, who is represented as a woman. A different and more erotic version can be found in 11QPsaa. 13: Travels, cf. 34.11; 39.4. 14: Wisdom is connected with the Temple as in 24.10. 23: House of instruction, a wisdom “school,” probably in Ben Sira's own house. 26: Bearing a yoke can be positive or negative in Sirach; see 6.23–31; 26.7; 28.19–20; 30.13; 33.27; 40.1. 28: Getting Wisdom through Ben Sira's teaching is connected with acquisition of wealth.

title: Deuteronomy
text:
Name
The standard English name of the book comes from the ancient Greek Septuagint (from deuteronomion, yielding Latin Deuteronomium), and means “Second Law.” That approach to naming the book represents the Greek translation of the Hebrew phrase Mishneh Torah found in Deuteronomy’s Law of the King, where it more properly means “a copy of the law” (see 17.18n.); indeed, the title Mishneh Torah is sometimes used for the book in rabbinic literature. The name Deuteronomy reflects the early Jewish perspective that the book is Moses’s rehearsal of the Torah; according to Deuteronomy, Moses, shortly before he dies, revisits the earlier laws and narratives of the Tetrateuch (the first four books of the Bible) and teaches Israel about them. The main Hebrew name of the book is Debarim (“words”), from the book’s opening, “These are the words” (1.1), following an ancient Near Eastern convention of naming books after their opening phrase.

title: Deuteronomy
text:
Authorship, Date, and Historical Context
Deuteronomy directly addresses the problem of the distance between past and present, between tradition and the needs of the contemporary generation, between revelation and interpretation. In that way, it is a remarkably modern text that instructs its audience in how to become more thoughtful readers of scripture. In narrative terms, Deuteronomy comes just as the Israelites, encamped on the plains of Moab, finally stand poised to enter the promised land. This entry into Canaan would provide the long‐awaited climax of the story that had begun with the promises to the ancestors in Genesis, and whose fulfillment had been delayed by the enslavement in Egypt and the wandering in the wilderness. Now, on the eve both of his death and of the nation’s entry into the land without him, Moses, as Deuteronomy’s speaker, interrupts the narrative action in order to deliver a series of three speeches (1.6–4.40; 5.1–28.68; 29.2–30.20), grouped together as a long farewell address. He reviews the nation’s history, expounds upon its laws, and instructs the people about the importance of loyalty to God. He also requires that the nation swear upon oath to uphold this combination of law and theological instruction as a covenant, one that supplements the prior covenant sworn at Horeb (the name for the mountain of revelation, called Sinai elsewhere; 29.1). Only after the conclusion of these discourses and a following appendix (chs 31–34) does the overall narrative line resume with the account of the nation’s entry into Canaan in the books of Joshua and Judges.
Despite the attribution of the text to Moses as its speaker, from the vantage point of modern biblical scholarship, Deuteronomy arose in its present form at a later period of Israelite history. The main sections of the book fit best in the seventh century bce as the composition of educated scribes associated with Jerusalem’s royal court. The striking similarities between the distinctive religious and legal requirements of Deuteronomy and the account of the major religious reform carried out by King Josiah of Judah in 622 bce (2 Kings 22–23) have long been recognized. That reform had been inspired by the discovery in the Temple of a “scroll of the Torah” (2 Kings 22.8; NRSV “book of the law”). Josiah’s reform restricted all sacrificial worship of God to Jerusalem and removed foreign elements from the system of worship; it culminated in the celebration of a nationally centralized passover at the Temple in Jerusalem (2 Kings 23.21–23). So strongly do these royal initiatives correspond to the distinctive requirements of Deuteronomy that scholars, both traditional and critical, have long identified the “scroll of the Torah” discovered in Josiah’s Temple as some form of the book of Deuteronomy.
Josiah’s reform, with Deuteronomy as its catalyst, was much more a revolution than a simple return to older forms of worship, as the book of Kings suggests. Previously, it had been entirely legitimate to sacrifice to God throughout the land, a principle reflected in biblical narratives such as Abraham at Shechem and near Bethel (Gen 12.7–8); Jacob at Bethel (Gen 35.1–7); Samuel at Mizpah, Ramah, Gilgal, and Bethlehem (1 Sam 7.9,17; 9.11–14; 10.8; 16.1–5); and Elijah upon Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18.20–46). Indeed, earlier biblical law stipulated that God would grant blessing “in every place where I [God] cause my name to be remembered” (Ex 20.24). Deuteronomy challenged that older norm, prohibiting sacrifice “at any place” (lit., “in every place”) and restricting it to a single site, implicitly Jerusalem (Deut 12.13–14). It is therefore striking that Deuteronomy presents itself as both an explication of the prior covenant (1.1–5) and as a supplement to it (29.1). Deuteronomy justifies itself in these two ways, yet neither description acknowledges the extent to which Deuteronomy actually challenges and revises earlier law in support of its new religious vision.
A century of Assyrian imperial domination serves as the historical background of Josiah’s reforms. The Northern Kingdom of Israel had fallen to the Assyrians in 722 bce (2 Kings 17). Continuing Assyrian incursions down the southeastern coast of the Mediterranean had all but reduced Judah to a rump‐state (2 Kings 18.13). In a desperate bid to preserve the nation’s autonomy, King Hezekiah of Judah made a pact with Assyria (2 Kings 18.13–18), as had his predecessor Ahaz (2 Kings 16.7–8). The resulting military allegiances may have led to religious syncretism, with foreign forms of worship introduced into the Temple (2 Kings 16.10–20; 21.1–6).
By the last quarter of the seventh century bce, Assyria’s might was in decline. In this context, Josiah’s religious reforms represented an important bid for Judean cultural, political, and religious autonomy. The monarch extended his reforms into the area of the former Northern Kingdom of Israel (2 Kings 23.15–20), territory formerly under Assyrian control. Deuteronomy, apparently written sometime during this historical crisis, likewise reflects the desire to preserve Judean cultural and religious integrity. Its authors were convinced that older conventions of worship and social organization were no longer viable. If the religion of the Lord was to survive the crisis, renewal and adaptation were necessary. The collection of laws that form the core of Deuteronomy (chs 12–26) provides a remarkably comprehensive program for cultural renewal. The laws deal with worship; the festival calendar; the major institutions of public life (justice, kingship, priesthood, prophecy); criminal, family, and civil law; and ethics. These laws are presented as the requirements of a covenant between God and the nation, which the people take an oath to uphold, upon penalty of sanctions, while maintaining unconditional loyalty to their God. That covenant structure closely corresponds to Neo‐Assyrian state treaties that have been recovered from this period, the most famous of which are the Vassal Treaties of Esarhaddon (672 bce). At a number of points, the authors of Deuteronomy seem consciously to have patterned their covenant after such treaties, treaties that had been repeatedly imposed upon Judah in the late eighth and seventh centuries bce. From this perspective, Deuteronomy is a countertreaty: Its authors turned the weapon of Assyrian imperialism into a bid for Judean independence, shifting its oath of loyalty from the Assyrian overlord to their divine sovereign.
The authors of Deuteronomy were thus tutored in international treaty conventions and elsewhere reveal their knowledge of the literary traditions of ancient Near Eastern law (see 15.1–18n.; 17.8–13n.,14–20n.; 22.13–30n.) and wisdom literature (1.13n.; 4.2n.). The authors of Deuteronomy made use of another common ancient Near Eastern convention as well. They did not directly attach their names to their compositions or write in their own voices; instead, they attributed their composition to a prestigious figure from the past. By employing Moses as their spokesperson, they established a link with tradition at precisely the time when tradition, for the sake of survival, had to be transformed. “Pseudepigraphy,” the convention of ascribing a text to an ancient personage, is particularly well known in the later literature of the Second Temple period; examples include Jubilees, 4 Ezra, the Testament of Abraham, and (among the Dead Sea Scrolls) the Temple Scroll.

title: Deuteronomy
text:
Literary History
Deuteronomy preserves several layers of tradition—the structure of three different speeches given by Moses, with an appendix, already suggests a process of literary growth. That growth is closely connected to the gradual formation of the Hebrew Bible. When Deuteronomy was first promulgated, it would not have been part of any larger whole. Instead, it would have stood by itself as a “scroll of the Torah” (“book of the law”). It would have consisted of most of the laws of chs 12–26, framed by a relatively simple introduction and conclusion. This form of Deuteronomy presented itself as a treaty concluded between the nation and its God in a formal ceremony whereby each citizen took an oath of under penalty of strict sanctions (28.1–46). This was very likely the preexilic form of Deuteronomy.
At a later stage, presumably sometime during the Exile in the mid‐sixth century bce, Deuteronomy would have been incorporated into the Deuteronomistic History (the books of Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings) to serve as its introduction. At this point, the Deuteronomistic editors would have given the book its literary frame (1.1–4.40; chs 31–34), while also adding to the collection of laws, selectively tying its promises or expectations to the later historical material. Expansions in Deuteronomy that reflect the Babylonian exile may derive from this stage (see 4.25–31; 28.47–56; 30.1–10).
At a still later point, in the exilic or postexilic period, Priestly editors appended Deuteronomy to the nascent Pentateuch to serve as its conclusion. Ironically, the decision to conclude the Pentateuch with Deuteronomy interrupted and delayed the logically expected climax of the larger narrative of Genesis through Numbers: the conquest of the land. This narrative climax was instead deferred to the books of Joshua and Judges. The final form of Deuteronomy also contains supplemental material that seems to reflect postexilic concerns.
In the final chapters of Deuteronomy, these three viewpoints (Deuteronomic, Deuteronomistic, and Priestly) operate simultaneously, creating a complex interplay of perspectives. The legal section is brought to its conclusion with a formal ratification ceremony involving the swearing of an oath to assume the penalties for transgressing the covenant (chs 29–31). At the same time, other editors worked to embed Deuteronomy in the Deuteronomistic History. Still other editors tied the book to Genesis–Numbers and thus make the creation of Torah—no longer the occupation of the land—the climax of the newly created Pentateuch. The three perspectives operate concurrently, spinning like Ezekiel’s vision of “a wheel within a wheel” (Ezek 1.16).

title: Deuteronomy
text:
Interpretation
Deuteronomy challenges its readers actively to confront the problem of the relation between revelation and interpretation, and breaks down conventional boundaries between scripture and tradition. It makes paradox central to its structure: the book distinctively narrates the process of its own formation (31.1–12) while also anticipating its prior existence as a complete literary work (17.18; 28.58; 30.10). Interpretation is directly and indirectly a theme of Deuteronomy (see 1.5). At many points, the authors of Deuteronomy reinterpret earlier narratives (see 6.1n.) and laws (particularly from the Book of the Covenant or Covenant Code in Ex 20–23). Moreover, the process of the book’s editing intentionally preserves conflicting perspectives on a full range of issues central to Israelite religion: on whether the revelation of the Decalogue at Horeb was direct or required the mediation of Moses (5.5n.); on the stature of Moses relative to other prophets (34.10n.); on the nature of divine punishment for sin (5.9–10n.; 7.10n.); on whether God rules as head of a pantheon or is the only God who exists (4.7–8n., 15–31n., 35n.; 32.8n.); and even on Deuteronomy’s own setting in time and place (1.1n.; 2.12n.; 3.11n.). These mutually exclusive positions preserve an ongoing ancient debate about fundamental religious assumptions. The editors of Deuteronomy opted against closure: they preserved these different schools of thought. Accordingly, there is in Deuteronomy no access to God in the covenant without entering into this debate. The modern reader of Deuteronomy must become, like the authors of Deuteronomy, an interpreter.
Bernard M. Levinson

1 These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan—in the wilderness, on the plain opposite Suph, between Paran and Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Di‐zahab. 2(By the way of Mount Seir it takes eleven days to reach Kadesh‐barnea from Horeb.) 3In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses spoke to the Israelites just as the Lord had commanded him to speak to them. 4This was after he had defeated King Sihon of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, and King Og of Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth anda in Edrei. 5Beyond the Jordan in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to expound this law as follows:
6The Lord our God spoke to us at Horeb, saying, “You have stayed long enough at this mountain. 7Resume your journey, and go into the hill country of the Amorites as well as into the neighboring regions—the Arabah, the hill country, the Shephelah, the Negeb, and the seacoast—the land of the Canaanites and the Lebanon, as far as the great river, the river Euphrates. 8See, I have set the land before you; go in and take possession of the land that Ia swore to your ancestors, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give to them and to their descendants after them.”
9At that time I said to you, “I am unable by myself to bear you. 10The Lord your God has multiplied you, so that today you are as numerous as the stars of heaven. 11May the Lord, the God of your ancestors, increase you a thousand times more and bless you, as he has promised you! 12But how can I bear the heavy burden of your disputes all by myself? 13Choose for each of your tribes individuals who are wise, discerning, and reputable to be your leaders.” 14You answered me, “The plan you have proposed is a good one.” 15So I took the leaders of your tribes, wise and reputable individuals, and installed them as leaders over you, commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, commanders of tens, and officials, throughout your tribes. 16I charged your judges at that time: “Give the members of your community a fair hearing, and judge rightly between one person and another, whether citizen or resident alien. 17You must not be partial in judging: hear out the small and the great alike; you shall not be intimidated by anyone, for the judgment is God’s. Any case that is too hard for you, bring to me, and I will hear it.” 18So I charged you at that time with all the things that you should do.
19Then, just as the Lord our God had ordered us, we set out from Horeb and went through all that great and terrible wilderness that you saw, on the way to the hill country of the Amorites, until we reached Kadeshbarnea. 20I said to you, “You have reached the hill country of the Amorites, which the Lord our God is giving us. 21See, the Lord your God has given the land to you; go up, take possession, as the Lord, the God of your ancestors, has promised you; do not fear or be dismayed.”
22All of you came to me and said, “Let us send men ahead of us to explore the land for us and bring back a report to us regarding the route by which we should go up and the cities we will come to.” 23The plan seemed good to me, and I selected twelve of you, one from each tribe. 24They set out and went up into the hill country, and when they reached the Valley of Eshcol they spied it out 25and gathered some of the land’s produce, which they brought down to us. They brought back a report to us, and said, “It is a good land that the Lord our God is giving us.”
26But you were unwilling to go up. You rebelled against the command of the Lord your God; 27you grumbled in your tents and said, “It is because the Lord hates us that he has brought us out of the land of Egypt, to hand us over to the Amorites to destroy us. 28Where are we headed? Our kindred have made our hearts melt by reporting, ‘The people are stronger and taller than we; the cities are large and fortified up to heaven! We actually saw there the offspring of the Anakim!’” 29I said to you, “Have no dread or fear of them. 30The Lord your God, who goes before you, is the one who will fight for you, just as he did for you in Egypt before your very eyes, 31and in the wilderness, where you saw how the Lord your God carried you, just as one carries a child, all the way that you traveled until you reached this place. 32But in spite of this, you have no trust in the Lord your God, 33who goes before you on the way to seek out a place for you to camp, in fire by night, and in the cloud by day, to show you the route you should take.”
34When the Lord heard your words, he was wrathful and swore: 35“Not one of these—not one of this evil generation—shall see the good land that I swore to give to your ancestors, 36except Caleb son of Jephunneh. He shall see it, and to him and to his descendants I will give the land on which he set foot, because of his complete fidelity to the Lord.” 37Even with me the Lord was angry on your account, saying, “You also shall not enter there. 38Joshua son of Nun, your assistant, shall enter there; encourage him, for he is the one who will secure Israel’s possession of it. 39And as for your little ones, who you thought would become booty, your children, who today do not yet know right from wrong, they shall enter there; to them I will give it, and they shall take possession of it. 40But as for you, journey back into the wilderness, in the direction of the Red Sea.”a
41You answered me, “We have sinned against the Lord! We are ready to go up and fight, just as the Lord our God commanded us.” So all of you strapped on your battle gear, and thought it easy to go up into the hill country. 42The Lord said to me, “Say to them, ‘Do not go up and do not fight, for I am not in the midst of you; otherwise you will be defeated by your enemies.’” 43Although I told you, you would not listen. You rebelled against the command of the Lord and presumptuously went up into the hill country. 44The Amorites who lived in that hill country then came out against you and chased you as bees do. They beat you down in Seir as far as Hormah. 45When you returned and wept before the Lord, the Lord would neither heed your voice nor pay you any attention.

2 46After you had stayed at Kadesh as many days as you did,1we journeyed back into the wilderness, in the direction of the Red Sea,a as the Lord had told me and skirted Mount Seir for many days. 2Then the Lord said to me: 3“You have been skirting this hill country long enough. Head north, 4and charge the people as follows: You are about to pass through the territory of your kindred, the descendants of Esau, who live in Seir. They will be afraid of you, so, be very careful 5not to engage in battle with them, for I will not give you even so much as a foot’s length of their land, since I have given Mount Seir to Esau as a possession. 6You shall purchase food from them for money, so that you may eat; and you shall also buy water from them for money, so that you may drink. 7Surely the Lord your God has blessed you in all your undertakings; he knows your going through this great wilderness. These forty years the Lord your God has been with you; you have lacked nothing.” 8So we passed by our kin, the descendants of Esau who live in Seir, leaving behind the route of the Arabah, and leaving behind Elath and Ezion‐geber.



The circuit via Transjordan


When we had headed out along the route of the wilderness of Moab, 9the Lord said to me: “Do not harass Moab or engage them in battle, for I will not give you any of its land as a possession, since I have given Ar as a possession to the descendants of Lot.” 10(The Emim—a large and numerous people, as tall as the Anakim—had formerly inhabited it. 11Like the Anakim, they are usually reckoned as Rephaim, though the Moabites call them Emim. 12Moreover, the Horim had formerly inhabited Seir, but the descendants of Esau dispossessed them, destroying them and settling in their place, as Israel has done in the land that the Lord gave them as a possession.) 13“Now then, proceed to cross over the Wadi Zered.”
So we crossed over the Wadi Zered. 14And the length of time we had traveled from Kadesh‐barnea until we crossed the Wadi Zered was thirty‐eight years, until the entire generation of warriors had perished from the camp, as the Lord had sworn concerning them. 15Indeed, the Lord’s own hand was against them, to root them out from the camp, until all had perished.
16Just as soon as all the warriors had died off from among the people, 17the Lord spoke to me, saying, 18“Today you are going to cross the boundary of Moab at Ar. 19When you approach the frontier of the Ammonites, do not harass them or engage them in battle, for I will not give the land of the Ammonites to you as a possession, because I have given it to the descendants of Lot.” 20(It also is usually reckoned as a land of Rephaim. Rephaim formerly inhabited it, though the Ammonites call them Zamzummim, 21a strong and numerous people, as tall as the Anakim. But the Lord destroyed them from before the Ammonites so that they could dispossess them and settle in their place. 22He did the same for the descendants of Esau, who live in Seir, by destroying the Horim before them so that they could dispossess them and settle in their place even to this day. 23As for the Avvim, who had lived in settlements in the vicinity of Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came from Caphtor, destroyed them and settled in their place.) 24“Proceed on your journey and cross the Wadi Arnon. See, I have handed over to you King Sihon the Amorite of Heshbon, and his land.
