title: Wisdom of Solomon
text:
18


But for your holy ones there was very great light.
Their enemiesa heard their voices but did not see their forms,
and counted them happy for not having suffered,
2and were thankful that your holy ones,b though previously wronged, were doing them no injury;
and they begged their pardon for having been at variance with them.b
3Therefore you provided a flaming pillar of fire
as a guide for your people'sc unknown journey,
and a harmless sun for their glorious wandering.
4For their enemiesd deserved to be deprived of light and imprisoned in darkness,
those who had kept your children imprisoned,
through whom the imperishable light of the law was to be given to the world.


5When they had resolved to kill the infants of your holy ones,
and one child had been abandoned and rescued,
you in punishment took away a multitude of their children;
and you destroyed them all together by a mighty flood.
6That night was made known beforehand to our ancestors,
so that they might rejoice in sure knowledge of the oaths in which they trusted.
7The deliverance of the righteous and the destruction of their enemies
were expected by your people.
8For by the same means by which you punished our enemies
you called us to yourself and glorified us.
9For in secret the holy children of good people offered sacrifices,
and with one accord agreed to the divine law,
so that the saints would share alike the same things,
both blessings and dangers;
and already they were singing the praises of the ancestors.a
10But the discordant cry of their enemies echoed back,
and their piteous lament for their children was spread abroad.
11The slave was punished with the same penalty as the master,
and the commoner suffered the same loss as the king;
12and they all together, by the one formb of death,
had corpses too many to count.
For the living were not sufficient even to bury them,
since in one instant their most valued children had been destroyed.
13For though they had disbelieved everything because of their magic arts,
yet, when their firstborn were destroyed, they acknowledged your people to be God's child.
14For while gentle silence enveloped all things,
and night in its swift course was now half gone,
15your all-powerful word leaped from heaven, from the royal throne,
into the midst of the land that was doomed,
a stern warrior
16carrying the sharp sword of your authentic command,
and stood and filled all things with death,
and touched heaven while standing on the earth.
17Then at once apparitions in dreadful dreams greatly troubled them,
and unexpected fears assailed them;
18and one here and another there, hurled down half dead,
made known why they were dying;
19for the dreams that disturbed them forewarned them of this,
so that they might not perish without knowing why they suffered.


20The experience of death touched also the righteous,
and a plague came upon the multitude in the desert,
but the wrath did not long continue.
21For a blameless man was quick to act as their champion;
he brought forward the shield of his ministry,
prayer and propitiation by incense;
he withstood the anger and put an end to the disaster,
showing that he was your servant.
22He conquered the wrathc not by strength of body,
not by force of arms,
but by his word he subdued the avenger,
appealing to the oaths and covenants given to our ancestors.
23For when the dead had already fallen on one another in heaps,
he intervened and held back the wrath,
and cut off its way to the living.
24For on his long robe the whole world was depicted,
and the glories of the ancestors were engraved on the four rows of stones,
and your majesty was on the diadem upon his head.
25To these the destroyer yielded, these hea feared;
for merely to test the wrath was enough.
crumbs: The Apocryphal/Deuterocanonical Books are listed here in four groupings, as follows:
(A) Books and Additions To Esther and Daniel That are In The Roman Catholic, Greek, and Slavonic Bibles

title: Wisdom of Solomon
text:
19


But the ungodly were assailed to the end by pitiless anger,
for Godb knew in advance even their future actions:
2how, though they themselves had permittedc your people to depart
and hastily sent them out,
they would change their minds and pursue them.
3For while they were still engaged in mourning,
and were lamenting at the graves of their dead,
they reached another foolish decision,
and pursued as fugitives those whom they had begged and compelled to leave.
4For the fate they deserved drew them on to this end,
and made them forget what had happened,
in order that they might fill up the punishment that their torments still lacked,
5and that your people might experienced an incredible journey,
but they themselves might meet a strange death.


6For the whole creation in its nature was fashioned anew,
complying with your commands,
so that your childrene might be kept unharmed.
7The cloud was seen overshadowing the camp,
and dry land emerging where water had stood before,
an unhindered way out of the Red Sea,
and a grassy plain out of the raging waves,
8where those protected by your hand passed through as one nation,
after gazing on marvelous wonders.
9For they ranged like horses,
and leaped like lambs,
praising you, O Lord, who delivered them.
10For they still recalled the events of their sojourn,
how instead of producing animals the earth brought forth gnats,
and instead of fish the river spewed out vast numbers of frogs.
11Afterward they saw also a new kindf of birds,
when desire led them to ask for luxurious food;
12for, to give them relief, quails came up from the sea.


13The punishments did not come upon the sinners
without prior signs in the violence of thunder,
for they justly suffered because of their wicked acts;
for they practiced a more bitter hatred of strangers.
14Others had refused to receive strangers when they came to them,
but these made slaves of guests who were their benefactors.
15And not only so—but, while punishment of some sort will come upon the former
for having received strangers with hostility,
16the latter, having first received them with festal celebrations,
afterward afflicted with terrible sufferings
those who had already shared the same rights.
17They were stricken also with loss of sight—
just as were those at the door of the righteous man—
when, surrounded by yawning darkness,
all of them tried to find the way through their own doors.


18For the elements changeda places with one another,
as on a harp the notes vary the nature of the rhythm,
while each note remains the same.b
This may be clearly inferred from the sight of what took place.
19For land animals were transformed into water creatures,
and creatures that swim moved over to the land.
20Fire even in water retained its normal power,
and water forgot its fire-quenching nature.
21Flames, on the contrary, failed to consume
the flesh of perishable creatures that walked among them,
nor did they meltc the crystalline, quick-melting kind of heavenly food.


22For in everything, O Lord, you have exalted and glorified your people,
and you have not neglected to help them at all times and in all places.





1.1–6.21: Exhortation to love righteousness. This opening section embodies a complex argument for justice in an elegant concentric structure:



A. Address to judges: "love righteousness" (1.1–15)

B. The erroneous reasoning of the ungodly (1.16–2.24)

C. In defense of virtue and justice (3.1–4.20)
The just are in the hand of God (3.1–13a)
The moral strength of the virtuous (3.13b–4.6)
Tws youth (4.7–20)





B’. The confession of the ungodly and the final judgment (5.1–23)



A’. Address to kings: "learn wisdom" (6.1–21)




1.1–15: Exhortation to love righteousness. A series of oppositions form the basis of making a choice for justice. On one side are righteousness, the Lord, God, wisdom, a holy and disciplined spirit, a kindly spirit, and the spirit of the Lord (vv. 1–7). On the other side are perverse thoughts, a deceitful soul, foolish thoughts, unrighteousness, blasphemers, and death (vv. 3–13). These oppositions are a version of the doctrine of the two ways (e.g., Ps 1). 1: The book begins with the literary device of the apostrophe, a direct address to the hearers or readers, though the actual audience is the Hellenistic Jewish community, not their Gentile rulers. 7: Wisdom seems to be equated with the spirit of the Lord. 11: Tongue, the dangers of rash speech is a frequent topic in wisdom literature (e.g., Prov 2.12; 4.24; 10.11, 18–19, 31–32; Sir 9.18; 20.24–26; 28.12–26). 12: Death here is not simply the experience of mortality but rather a total annihilation and separation from God. 14: Hades, both the abode of the dead in Greek tradition, and the god who presides over the underworld.


1.16–2.24: The erroneous reasoning of the ungodly. In the style of the Greco-Roman diatribe, the author creates a fictional adversary, “the ungodly,” who embody the reasoning for injustice which the author will refute in subsequent texts. The section condenses arguments used to justify exploiting the weak. It apparently evokes the Epicurean insistence on materiality and enjoyment in life, but it is a fictional caricature of Epicurean thought, which also valued moderation. 1.16: Covenant with death (lit., “him”; see v.14n.), cf. Isa 28.15. 2.1–5: The negative judgment on life might be construed as imitating the descriptions of the brevity of human life elsewhere in the Bible (e.g., Pss 90.9–10; 102.3,11; Job 10.20; 14.1–2; Eccl 6.12), but an underlying despair about the valuelessness of life underscores a sinister judgment. 2.1: Hades, see 1.14n. 2.6–24: The ungodly move from the exhortation to enjoy life (vv. 6–9) to the counsel of exploiting their power over others (2.10–11), to opposing the righteous who are in conflict with their ideas (vv. 12–19), and finally with the counsel to brutally execute the just one who stood against them (v. 20). 10–20: These verses evoke the “suffering servant” of Isa 52.13-53.12; cf. especially vv. 19–20 and Isa 53.7–9. The term child (Gk “pais”) in vv. 13,18 can also be translated as “servant.” 21–24: The mistake in the reasoning of the ungodly is found in their opening judgment on the meaning of human life. God has created human beings not arbitrarily but for immortality. The devil's envy, likely a reference to the serpent in the garden of Eden (Gen 3).


3.1–4.20: In defense of virtue and justice. In three diptychs the author contrasts the reality of immortal life for the righteous with the mere appearance of power in the life of the ungodly.


3.1–13a: The first diptych: the just are in the hand of God. The first diptych counters the final judgment of the wicked against the just who are tested with a shameful death (2.12–20). Only from the perspective of the ungodly is the death of the virtuous considered a tragedy. In reality, they had been tested by God and found worthy (cf. Deut 8.2–5; Ps 17.3). 1: Souls, the author repeatedly emphasizes the primacy of the soul in constituting human identity (1.4,11; 2.22; 3.13; 4.14; 7.27; 8.10; 9.15; 10.16; 15.8,11). The hand of God alludes to the power of God. 4: Immortality rather than bodily resurrection reflects Greek influence (1.15; 2.23; 4.1; 6.18–19; 8.13,17; 12.1; 15.3; cf. 2 Esd 2.45; 7.13,96; 8.54; 4 Macc 9.22). 6: Like gold in the furnace, cf. Zech 13.9; Ps 66.10; Prov 17.3; Sir 2.5; like a sacrificial burnt offering, cf. Gen 8.21. 7–8: Shine forth … govern, in apocalyptic literature the glory of the virtuous is often described as starlike brilliance (e.g., Dan 12.3; Matt 13.43) and as rulership (e.g., Dan 7.27). 9: Grace and mercy, his elect, in Wisdom, the reward of immortality is fashioned more from the covenantal promises to Israel than from Greek philosophy. 10–13a: The connection between the way one sins and the way one is punished is a principle which will be applied in the plague narrative of the Exodus from Egypt (11.16; 12.23–27; 14.30–31). A similar relationship appears in several psalms of lament (e.g., Pss 7.15–16; 9.15; 35.8; 37.14–15; 141.10). Foolish wives and accursed offspring, these concluding images of judgment introduce the next diptych which contrasts the apparent lack of fruit of the virtuous with the apparent abundant fruit of the ungodly.


3.13b–4.6: The second diptych: the moral strength of the virtuous. This central diptych counters the argument of the ungodly, who declared their might to be their law of right and what is weak to be useless (2.10–11). 13b–15: Blessed is the barren woman.. the eunuch. The lack of children was often considered a grave misfortune if not a curse (cf. Gen 30.23; 1 Sam 1.4–8). The eunuch was barred from both the priesthood and the assembly of the Lord (cf. Lev 21.20; Deut 23.2). Wisdom overturns these judgments on the basis of virtue. The virtuous barren woman will have much fruit at the time of God's visitation (cf. Isa 54.1), and the eunuch who has avoided evil will have a place in the Temple (cf. Isa 56.3–4). 16–19: In contrast, children of adulterers will have a grievous end. The illicit gains of injustice are ephemeral (cf. Job 20). 4.1: Childlessness with virtue, cf. Sir 16.3; Prov 10.7. Memory, traditionally associated with blessing and transcendence of death (cf. 8.13; Ps 112.6: Prov 10.7; Sir 44.8–15; 2 Esd 12.47). 3-5: Cf. Sir 23.22–27. For the imagery, cf. Job 15.32–34; Ps 1.4–5; Ezek 17.9; 31.10–14; Dan 4.14.


4.7–20: The third diptych: early death of a virtuous youth. The final diptych counters the first argument of the ungodly (2.1–9). 7–10: The virtuous youth who dies early is better off than the ungodly who reach old age; cf. Isa 57.1–2. 11: They were caught up, an allusion to Enoch, taken up by God (Gen 5.24, cf. Sir 44.16; Heb 11.5). Gen. Rab. 25.1 claims that the purpose of Enoch's removal was to preserve his character. 12: Roving desire, see 15.5–6; Eccl 6.9; 11.9; Sir 18.30–19.3. 16–19: The righteous will condemn the ungodly, an allusion to Daniel, a holy youth who confounds the wicked elders and saves Susanna (Sus 45–62). 18: The Lord will laugh, cf. Ps 2.4; Prov 1.26. 18.b–19: For similar threats see Isa 13.6–16; 24.17–23; 66.24; Jer 15.7–9. 20: Their lawless deeds will convict them, a parallel to the conclusion of the second diptych in which the children of the ungodly witness against their parents (4.6).


5.1–14: The confession of the ungodly. The sudden unexpected appearance of the just before their oppressors elicits from the ungodly an admission of their folly; cf. Isa 52.13–53.12. The use of an imaginary monologue, here and in 2.1–20, is a device common in diatribe. 5: The children of God, the ungodly had mocked the claim of the just to be God's child (2.18). 6–14: Admission of guilt by the wicked. 6: The metaphor of path or way for conduct is common in wisdom literature (e.g., Job 22.15; Ps 1.1; Prov 4.14-19). 9–14: The ephemeral existence of the ungodly; cf. Job 20.4–29; Ps 1.4–5; 2 Esd 7.61; Jas 4.14. 10–11: A ship … a bird, cf. Prov 30.18–19.


5.15–23: The final judgment. In contrast to the ungodly whose life is dispersed into nothingness, the righteous live forever in the presence of the Lord. 16: Crown … diadem, the reward of the just is often depicted as royal; cf. Prov 4.9; Isa 28.5. 17–22: For the image of God taking zeal as armor see Isa 59.17–19, but that God will arm all creation (v. 20) is unusual; cf. Sir 39.28–31. Creation's collaboration with God will be a major theme in chs 11–19.


6.1–21 Address to kings: “learn wisdom.” This exhortation parallels the opening exhortation for rulers to love righteousness (1.1–15). Death is the result of injustice (1.16). The idea of rulers needing instruction in order to rule with justice is a familiar theme both in Greek philosophical treaties (e.g., Plato, The Republic; Plutarch, To an Uneducated Ruler) and in biblical texts; cf. 1 Kings 3.1–28, where King Solomon asks for a discerning mind in order to rule justly. 1: An apostrophe, see 1.1n. 3: Political authority is granted by God (cf. Prov 8.15–16; Jer 27.5–7; Dan 2.37–38; 4.17. 4–6: For God's judgment against the mighty, cf. 1 Sam 2.3–5; Job 34.24–30; Ps 2; Isa 2.11–17; Jer 25.15–29; Sir 10.8–18. 12–16: Wisdom is found by those who seek her, because she seeks out those who are worthy (v. 16, cf. Prov 8.17; Sir 6.27). The figure of Wisdom occurs frequently in late Israelite and early Jewish literature, especially Prov 1.20–33; 8; 9.1–6; Job 28.12–28; Sir 1.1–27; 4.11–19; 6.18–37; 14.20–15.10; 24; Bar 3.9–4.4. 17–20: The exhortation concludes with a literary form called a “sorites” in Greek, a logical chain-syllogism, which consists of a series of statements readily acceptable but leading to a surprise conclusion. Each statement picks up the last key element from the previous one. The surprise conclusion here is that the desire for wisdom leads to a kingdom. 21: This concluding exhortation to honor wisdom introduces the second major section of the book, which focuses primarily on the attributes of wisdom.


6.22–11.1: Praise of the wisdom of God.  


6.22–25: I will tell you, for the first time the author speaks in the first person and continues to do so through ch 9, promising to reveal to readers the mysteries of wisdom. 22: Beginning of creation, see Prov 8.22–31.


7.1–9.18: The implied author speaks in the persona of King Solomon and describes his life and search for wisdom.


7.1–8.21: The concentric framework of Solomon's narrative:



A. Birth and mortality of Solomon (7.1–6)

B. Wisdom is greater than any other good (7.7–12)

C. God knows wisdom and imparts knowledge (7.13–22a)

D. Eulogy of wisdom (7.22b–8.1)



C’. Solomon desires wisdom (8.2–9)



B’. Wisdom grants fame and success (8.10–16)



A’. As a child, Solomon recognizes that only God is the giver of wisdom (8.17–21).




7.1–6 : Solomon acknowledges his solidarity with all humanity and offers a hopeful project in life that is the antithesis to that of the ungodly (2.1–20). 2: Ten months, implying lunar months, for a gestation period of forty weeks; compacted with blood, cf. Job 10.10; Ps 139.13–16. 7–14: Based on 1 Kings 3.4–14; 2 Chr 1.6–12. 8–9: Priceless gem, cf. Job 28.12–19; Prov 2.4; 3.14–16. 12: She was their mother, cf. Prov 7.24; 8.32; Sir 15.2. 14: Friendship with God, cf. vv. 27–28; “friend of God” is one of the highest epithets that could be given to a person (Abraham, 2 Chr 20.7; Moses, Ex 33.11). 15–22a: Divine wisdom is associated not only with virtue but with all philosophical and scientific knowledge; cf. 1 Kings 4.29–34.


7.22b–8.1: Eulogy of wisdom, a presentation of the qualities of wisdom with two sets of lists. 7.22b–24 consists of twenty-one attributes (three sets of seven), mostly derived from Stoic philosophy highlighting the pervasiveness of wisdom in the cosmos. 7.25–8.1 includes a list of five metaphors, derived primarily from Greek philosophy, that illustrate the intimate relationship between God and wisdom: breath, emanation, reflection, mirror, image. 25: Breath, see 11.20; Sir 24.3. Emanation or effluence, cf. Cicero, The Nature of the Gods 2.79; Sir 1.9; 24.23–33. 26: Mirror, cf. 2 Cor 3.18; Philo, Quest. in Gen. 1.57. 27–28: Friends of God, see 7.14n. 7.29–8.1: For wisdom's excellence over the constellations and light itself, cf. 7.10,26.


8.2–16: The extended metaphor of Solomon pursuing wisdom to be his bride. The erotic metaphor for wisdom has a precedent in Prov 9.1–6; Sir 51.13–22. A more explicitly erotic version of Sir 51 occurs in 11QPsa. Cf. also the relationship of God and Israel as husband and wife (Isa 62.4–5; Hos 2.14–23). 4: Associate in his works, cf. Prov 8.22–31. 5–9: Four conditional sentences highlight wisdom's superiority over common values to be pursued. 7: The values wisdom embodies include the four cardinal virtues: self-control, prudence, justice, courage; see Plato, Republic 443D–E, 444D). 13: I shall have immortality, cf. 3.4; 4.1; 6.18–19.


8.17–21: God is the giver of the gift of wisdom. 17: Immortality, see 8.13n. 18: Friendship, see 7.14n. 19–20: A good soul … or rather, being good, the preexistence of the soul championed in Greek thought is reflected here, but greater emphasis is placed on the moral disposition of the person. Cf. Philo, Giants 6–14; 2 En. 23.4–5. 21. Unless God gave her to me, cf. Sir 1.1.


9.1–18: Solomon prays to God for wisdom. The prayer builds on 1 Kings 3.6–9 and 2 Chr 1.8–10 where Solomon speaks with God in a dream and in a vision. It is composed in an elegant concentric structure:



A. Address to judges: “love righteousness” (1.1–15)

B. The erroneous reasoning of the ungodly (1.16–2.24)

C. In defense of virtue and justice (3.1–4.20)
The just are in the hand of God (3.1–13a)
The moral strength of the virtuous (3.13b–4.6)
The early death of a virtuous youth (4.7–20)





B’. The confession of the ungodly and the final judgment (5.1–23)



A’. Address to kings: “learn wisdom” (6.1–21)




1: By your word; cf. Gen 1.3, etc.; Sir 42.15. 2–3: Cf. Gen 1.28; 2.7. 4: By your throne, personified wisdom is intimately bound to God; cf. v. 10; Prov 8.27–30; Sir 24.4. 5–6: Solomon's weakness as a motive for his plea for wisdom; cf. 7.1–7; 14.17. 7–8: King … judge, cf. 1 Kings 1.28–40; 3.7; for his responsibility to build a temple, cf. 2 Sam 7.13; 1 Kings 5.19; Sir 47.13. On the earthly temple as a copy of the heavenly temple, see Heb 8.5. 9–11: Cf. Solomon's petition with wisdom's self-description in Prov 8.4–21,27–30. 12: My father, King David; 2 Sam 12.24. 13: Cf. Isa 40.12–14; Sir 1.2–6; Bar 3.29–31. 15–17: That the perishable body weighs down the soul was a common Greek notion (cf. Plato, Phaedr. 81C) and reiterates Solomon's acknowledgment of human weakness. The five rhetorical questions in vv. 13–17 emphasizing the limits of human knowledge and ability are all undone by the gift of God's wisdom and spirit. 18: Saved by wisdom, a perspective found here for the first time in scripture and developed in the following chapters (cf. Wis 10.4); normally God is the savior (cf. Ex 14.30; Deut 33.29; 1 Sam 17.37; 2 Chr 32.22). Although wisdom is the savior of the righteous ancestors in ch 10, God returns as the protagonist who saves Israel in the latter part of the book (cf. Wis 16.7).


10.1–11.1: Wisdom saves the righteous ancestors. As examples of wisdom's power to save, the author provides seven loose contrasts in which the righteous were saved through wisdom whereas the wicked perished for lack of wisdom. Names are not provided in order to engage the reader in identifying the various personages. 1–2: The first-formed father, Adam, is not called righteous, for he was saved by wisdom from his transgression; this does not exactly appear in Gen 2–3. 3: Cain (Gen 4.1–16). 4: The sin of Cain in killing his brother is named as the cause of the flood; cf. Gen 6.11. The righteous man, Noah; cf. Gen 6–9. 5: The nations … confusion, at the tower of Babel, Gen 11.1–9. The righteous man, Abraham, cf. Gen 15.6; compassion for his child, Isaac, Gen 22.1–19. 6: A righteous man, though in Gen 19 Lot is not presented in exemplary fashion, the author interprets the two angels who save him as the work of wisdom. The ungodly … the Five Cities, Sodom, Gomorrah, and the other cities of the Plain; Gen 19.1–29. 7: A pillar of salt, Lot's wife; Gen 19.26. 10–12: Jacob. Several events from Jacob's life are alluded to: flight from his brother Esau, Gen 27.41–45; Jacob's vision of the ladder at Bethel, the kingdom of God, Gen 28.10–17; Jacob's prosperity despite his oppressors, Laban and his sons, Gen 30.25–31.54; Jacob's wrestling with an angel in arduous contest at Peniel, Gen 32.22–32. 13–14: Joseph. Several events from Joseph's life are singled out from the lengthy narrative: being sold by his brothers, Gen 37.28; the unsuccessful seduction by Potiphar's wife (delivered from sin), Gen 39.6–20; being liberated from the prison, Gen 41.1–43; and Joseph's rise to power (scepter of a kingdom), Gen 41.37–57. 15–21: A holy people, Israel. A nation of oppressors, Egypt, when it oppressed the Israelites (Ex 1.8–14). The final contrast is more complex than the previous in that the righteous consists of the entire people of Israel and their singular leader, Moses. 16: Servant of the Lord, a frequent title for Moses (e.g., Ex 14.31; Num 12.7; Deut 34.5). 17: Shelter … starry flame, Ex 13.21–22. 18–19: The Red Sea, the only proper name mentioned in the book, Ex 14–15. 20: Plundered the ungodly, Ex 11.2; 12.35–36; sang hymns, Ex 15.1–21. 11.1: By the holy prophet, with this final reference to wisdom prospering the righteous through the hand of Moses, wisdom recedes into the background.


11.2–19.22: The Exodus and divine providence. Wisdom recedes into the background, while God is the protagonist who rewards the righteous and thwarts the godless. The proposition from the first part of the book, that God will “arm creation to repel his enemies” (5.17–23) is confirmed throughout this section. The section also exhibits the principle that the sins of the godless contain the seeds of their own punishment. Reflections on divine mercy and the source of idolatry are prominent themes. The entire reflection is ultimately folded into direct praise to God for the providential care of the just (10.20–21; 11.17–26; 19.22).


11.1–14: First contrast: plague of the Nile and water from the rock. 1: Holy prophet, Moses; cf. Deut 18:15; 34:10. 5–9: Through the very things, the inherent relationship between sin and punishment. The Egyptians drowned the Israelite infants in the Nile (11.7; cf. Ex 1.22) and were punished by the Nile becoming undrinkable (11.6; cf. Ex 7.14–24). In turn the Israelites received abundant water (Ex 17.1–7; Num 20.2–13). 8–10: The thirst of the righteous as divine pedagogy (cf. 3.3–7; Deut 8.2–5).


11.15–16.1–4: Second contrast: plague of irrational creatures versus the gift of quails. 11.15–16: Egyptian gods were often depicted with animal features; hence the plague of various animals (Ex 8.1–19; 9.1–7). Two theological reflections interrupt the contrast, which resumes in 16.1.


11.17–12.27: First theological reflection: the power and mercy of God. The reflection contrasts the manner in which God punishes: Egyptians are punished so that they repent (11.17–12.2), the Canaanites are punished moderately (12.3–18), the Israelites are punished mildly so that they learn to be merciful (12.19–22), and finally the Egyptians are punished so as to recognize the true God (12.23–27).


11.17–12.2: The moderation of God toward Egyptians. 17: Formless matter, a term borrowed from Greek philosophy (see Plato, Timaeus 50D-E); cf. the “formless void” of Gen 1.2). 20: Measure … number … weight, see Plato, Philebus 55E, Republic 602D. 12.1–2: Your immortal spirit is in all things, cf. 7.24–25; 15.11; Gen 2.7.


12.3–18: The moderation of God toward Canaanites, as an example of God's moderation toward sinners. 2: The purpose of punishment is rehabilitation; cf. 11.23. 4–8: Their detestable practices, see Lev 18.21–29; Deut 12.31; 18.10–12. 8: Wasps, see Ex 23.28; Deut 7.20; Josh 24.12. 13: Any god besides you, see Deut 32.39; Isa 44.6; cf. Ex 20.3.


12.19–22: Israel is to be merciful and to trust. 19: The manner of God's punishment of others and of Israel is a lesson to be emulated and grounds for hope.


12.23–27: The sins and punishments of Egypt. The very animals worshiped by the Egyptians became the instruments of the plagues; see 11.15–16n.; 15.18–19. 27: The true God, cf. Ex 12.31–32.


13.1–15.19: Second theological reflection: false worship. Three critiques: of philosophers who worship the natural world (13.1–9); of the worship of idols (13.10–15.13); of the enemies of Israel who worship both idols and odious animals (15.14–19).


13.1–9: The natural world. 1: Although Platonists considered the Supreme Being (the one who exists) as separate from the material creator, for Jews the Supreme Being is the same as the artisan of creation. 2–5: Fire, wind, air … luminaries … the elements of nature and the luminaries in the sky; see Deut 4.19; 17.3; 2 Kings 17.16; Job 31.26–28. 6–9: Worshipers of nature receive the least blame because they continue seeking God within the cosmos which is God's creation.


13.10–15.13: Polemic against idolatry. Idolatry is more blameworthy because idolaters worship human-made artifacts. For other critiques against idolatry see Pss 97.7; 115.3–8; 135.15–18; Isa 2.8–20; 40.18–20; 44.9–20; 45.16–20; 46.5–7; Jer 10.1–16; Hab 2.18; Bar 6.8–73. The criticism is simplistic, since no pagans regarded themselves as worshiping a piece of wood, stone, or metal. The satire is aimed at a Jewish audience and is similar to comments about idols in some Greco-Roman writers (Horace, Satires 1.8.1–7; Sophocles, according to Strom. 5.14.113.1–2).


13.10–19: The critique notes both the substance for the making of idols and the form into which they are made. 11: Cf. Isa 40.18–20; Jer 10.3–5. 17–19: Cf. Ps 115.3–8.


14.1–11: During travels on ship, safety comes from God and not from wooden idols. 2: Wisdom was the artisan, see 9.9–11. 3: Your providence, cf. 17.2; 4 Macc 9.24. O Father, cf. Isa 64.8. 6–7: Arrogant giants, see Gen 6.1–5; Sir 16.7; Bar 3.26–28. Took refuge on a raft, Noah's ark; blessed is the wood, referring to the ark. 11: Visitation, God's judgment upon the idols, cf. 3.7, Ex 12.12; Isa 2.18–20.


14.12–31: The origin and consequences of idolatry. The idea that human beings could be elevated to divine status occurs in Egypt and Mesopotamia and became common in the Greco-Roman world. 12: Fornication, a metaphor for worshiping other gods; see Jer 3.6–8; Ezek 16.15–43; Hos 4.11–19, cf. Ex 34.15–17. 15–21: Two examples provide the origins of idolatry: a statue in memory of a dead child (vv. 15–16) and of a king made as a representation for subjects in distant lands (vv. 17–21). 22–31: The consequences of idolatry are all sorts of vices. 23: Cf. 12.5; Lev 18.21. 25: See Hos 4.1–2. 31: The just penalty, cf. 11.16.


15.1–6: True worship of God brings righteousness and immortality. 1: The description of God's mercy alludes to Ex 34.6–7.


15.7–13: Clay idols. The critique is parallel to that of the carpenter (13.10–19). There is a progressive downgrade in the quality of all the substances used for idols: gold, silver, stone, wood, clay. 8: That souls were borrowed was a philosophical conception (cf. 15.16).


15.14–19: Enemies of Israel who worship idols and hateful animals. 14: Most foolish, the Egyptians who oppressed the Israelites (Ex 1.8–12). 18–19: Egyptian animal worship, see 11.15–16n. Romans, as well as Jews, criticized the practice, cf. Juvenal, Satire 15.1–11; Philo, Decalogue 76–80.


16.1–4: Second contrast resumes from 11.15–16. 1: Tormented, cf. 11.15 and Ex 8.1–15, the first plague of animals. Several of the plagues are combined for the second and third contrasts. 2–4: Instead … quails, the contrasting benefit to the righteous during the journey in the wilderness; cf. Num 11.31–34, where the Israelites’ demand for meat is criticized.


16.5–14. Third contrast: insects that kill versus the saving brazen serpent. 5: The third contrast uniquely begins with the suffering of the Israelites; see Num 21.5–6. 6: A symbol of deliverance, the serpent of bronze Moses was asked to make, Num 21.7–9. 9: In Ex 8.12–28 and 10.12–20 the Egyptians do not die from the insects, but Josephus (Ant 2.14.3) includes this detail. 12: Your word … heals all, the bronze serpent is not an idol, since it is God who heals, not the bronze object, cf. 16.7.


16.15–29: Fourth contrast: plague of storms versus the gift of manna. 16: The seventh plague was destruction by rains … hail … storms, and fire, Ex 9.22–26. 20: In contrast, the righteous received food of angels, the manna in the wilderness, see Ex 16.1–21; Num 11.6–9. The contrast emphasizes the forces of the universe which attack the ungodly but help the righteous, cf. 8.4–6; 16.17,24; 19.18–21. 21: To suit everyone's liking, a tradition reflected in b. Yoma 75a; Mekilta on Ex 16.23. 26: So that your children … might learn, cf. Deut 8.2–5.


17.1–18.4: Fifth contrast: plague of darkness versus a pillar of fire. The plague enslaves the unrighteous (Ex 10.21–23) because they had sinned by enslaving the Israelites. The description of terrors is reminiscent of the literary genre known as the “descent into Hades,” see Virgil, Aeneid 6. 17.7: The delusions of their magic art, see Ex 7.22; 8.7, 18–19; 9.11. 14: Hades, see 1.14n. 17.20–18.3: A brilliant light … a great light … a flaming pillar of fire, see Ex 13.21–22; cf. Num 9.15–16; Ps 78.14; 105.39. 18.4: The law was to be given to the world, see Isa 2.2–3; Mic 4.1–4; 2 Esd 7.20–24; 14.20–22.


18.5–25: Sixth contrast: destruction of children versus the blameless man who stops the destroyer. The death of the Egyptian firstborn is contrasted with the saving power of Aaron. 5: Wisdom connects Ex 1.15–22 with Ex 12.29–30; cf. Wis 11.6–14. One child, Moses. Flood, Ex 14.26–29. 9: The first Passover (Ex 12.1–28). 15: Your all-powerful word … a stern warrior, the destroyer in Ex 12.23 is the punishing side of God. If … leaped from heaven, from the royal throne is a reference to wisdom (cf. 9.10), this would be the only example of wisdom having a punishing role. 20: The experience of death by the righteous, cf. the punishment for rebellion in the wilderness in Num 16.23–35. 21–25: The blameless man, Aaron, who saves the Israelites in Num 16.41–50. 24: See Ex 28.15–28. On the symbolism of the high priest's vestments, see Josephus, Ant. 3.7.7; Philo, Moses 2.117–26.


19.1–12: Seventh contrast: the strange death versus the extraordinary deliverance at the Red Sea. The final contrast sets the drowning of Pharaoh's army against the deliverance of the Israelites (Ex 14.1–31). 3: Foolish decision, cf. Ex 14.5–9. 6–12: A recapitulation of several plagues and blessings highlighting the way the cosmos thwarts the unjust and helps the righteous. 6: The whole creation … fashioned anew, see 5.17–23; 16.24. 7: Cloud, Ex 13.21. 10–12: See 16.1–4; cf. Ex 8.1–19.


19.13–22. Final theological reflection: the debilitating consequences of injustice; the transforming power of the cosmos; concluding doxology praising God. 13–17: Hatred of strangers, a new argument is introduced to justify the punishments. Egypt had welcomed Joseph and the Israelites as guests whom they enslaved, see Gen 46–47; Ex 1; righteous man, Lot; see 10.6n. 18–21: The analogy of musical harmony is used to explain the transformative capacity of the cosmos; see Plato, Republic 7.12.530; Cicero, The Nature of the Gods 3.39.92. Three of the four elements of Greek philosophy are present—earth (land), water, and fire. Air is perhaps represented through music. 19: Land animals, water creatures, an unusual depiction of the Israelites passing through the sea, 20: Fire, cf. 16,17–23.


22:A final doxology praising God, reaches back to the righteous who sang hymns to God and praised God's defending hand, 10.20–21. The entire history of deliverance from Egypt is engulfed into a single voice of praise to God for thwarting injustice and helping righteousness.

title: Zephaniah
section: Name, Canonical Location, and Date of Composition
text:
Name, Canonical Location, and Date of Composition
Zephaniah is the ninth of the twelve Minor Prophets in both the Masoretic Text (MT) and the Septuagint (LXX). Its superscription provides more detailed information than do those of Nahum and Habakkuk, the two books that precede it in the canon.

The superscription's four-generation genealogy links the prophet (whose name means “the Lord has hidden” or “the Lord has stored up”) with the reign of the Judean king Josiah (640–609 bce). Second Kings 22–23 lauds Josiah as one of Judah's great religious reformers; before his death in 609 bce, he removed foreign images from the Temple in Jerusalem, centralized worship practices, and established for Judah a degree of political independence from the Assyrian Empire. Resonating strongly with this narrative, Zephaniah blames Judeans for mixing worship of the Lord with the worship of other deities (1.4–5) and accuses the royal court of dressing in foreign attire (1.8–9).

While the literary setting of the book in the seventh century bce is obvious, the book may actually have been composed or at least substantially edited at a later date. The concluding promise of salvation for “daughter Jerusalem” (3.14–20), for example, reflects an exilic or postexilic perspective in its concern with the return of exiles to the city.

title: Zephaniah
text:
Contents and Interpretation
Much of Zephaniah mirrors other prophetic books. It opens with a dramatic announcement of “the day of the Lord,” a time in which God will act decisively to (re-)establish justice (Joel 1.15; 3.14; Am 5.18; Ob 15; Zech 12.4). It pairs oracles against foreign nations (cf. Isa 13–23; Jer 46–51; Ezek 25–32; Am 1.3–2.3) with oracles against Judah (cf. Isa 3; 5; Jer 1; 3; Am 2; Mic 2), accusing Judah of idolatry and injustice (cf. Isa 5.7; Jer 2.28; 11.13) and the nations of arrogance (cf. Isa 16.6; Jer 48.29; Zech 10.11). Zephaniah also ends with an announcement of salvation to “daughter Jerusalem,” similar to those found in other prophetic books (e.g., Mic 4; Zech 2; 9). Its opening chapter, however, is distinctive for its comprehensive and harrowing depiction of the devastation of the earth and its inhabitants. Through insistent repetition and allusions to the creation narratives, it delivers an all- encompassing litany of doom that remains one of the most enduring images of judgment from the Hebrew Bible.

The book's powerful language for divine judgment captivated the imagination of later interpreters. The Apocalypse of Zephaniah, a Jewish document usually dated between 100 bce and 70 ce, describes the prophet's tour of hell as well as his brief visit to heaven. The Dies irae (“day of wrath”), a thirteenth-century Christian sequence long included in the Mass for the Dead, quotes the Latin translation of Zephaniah 1.15. “Shoah,” the Hebrew word for ruin in 1.15, is now a designation for the devastation of European Jewry known as the Holocaust.
Julia M. O’Brien



1 The word of the Lord that came to Zephaniah son of Cushi son of Gedaliah son of Amariah son of Hezekiah, in the days of King Josiah son of Amon of Judah.


2I will utterly sweep away everything
  from the face of the earth, says the Lord.
3I will sweep away humans and animals;
  I will sweep away the birds of the air
  and the fish of the sea.
I will make the wicked stumble.a
  I will cut off humanity
  from the face of the earth, says the Lord.
4I will stretch out my hand against Judah,
  and against all the inhabitants of Jerusalem;
and I will cut off from this place every remnant of Baal
  and the name of the idolatrous priests;b
5those who bow down on the roofs
  to the host of the heavens;
those who bow down and swear to the Lord,
  but also swear by Milcom;c
6those who have turned back from following the Lord,
  who have not sought the Lord or inquired of him.
7Be silent before the Lord God!
  For the day of the Lord is at hand;
the Lord has prepared a sacrifice,
  he has consecrated his guests.
8And on the day of the Lord's sacrifice
I will punish the officials and the king's sons
  and all who dress themselves in foreign attire.
9On that day I will punish
  all who leap over the threshold,
who fill their master's house
  with violence and fraud.


10On that day, says the Lord,
  a cry will be heard from the Fish Gate,
a wail from the Second Quarter,
  a loud crash from the hills.
11The inhabitants of the Mortar wail,
  for all the traders have perished;
  all who weigh out silver are cut off.
12At that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps,
  and I will punish the people
who rest complacentlya on their dregs,
  those who say in their hearts,
“The Lord will not do good,
  nor will he do harm.”
13Their wealth shall be plundered,
  and their houses laid waste.
Though they build houses,
  they shall not inhabit them;
though they plant vineyards,
  they shall not drink wine from them.


14The great day of the Lord is near,
  near and hastening fast;
the sound of the day of the Lord is bitter,
  the warrior cries aloud there.
15That day will be a day of wrath,
  a day of distress and anguish,
a day of ruin and devastation,
  a day of darkness and gloom,
a day of clouds and thick darkness,
  16a day of trumpet blast and battle cry
against the fortified cities
  and against the lofty battlements.


17I will bring such distress upon people
  that they shall walk like the blind;
  because they have sinned against the Lord,
their blood shall be poured out like dust,
  and their flesh like dung.
18Neither their silver nor their gold
  will be able to save them
  on the day of the Lord's wrath;
in the fire of his passion
  the whole earth shall be consumed;
for a full, a terrible end
  he will make of all the inhabitants of the earth.

title: Zephaniah
text:
2


Gather together, gather,
  O shameless nation,
2before you are driven away
  like the drifting chaff,b
before there comes upon you
  the fierce anger of the Lord,
before there comes upon you
  the day of the Lord's wrath.
3Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land,
  who do his commands;
seek righteousness, seek humility;
  perhaps you may be hidden
  on the day of the Lord's wrath.
4For Gaza shall be deserted,
  and Ashkelon shall become a desolation;
Ashdod's people shall be driven out at noon,
  and Ekron shall be uprooted.


5Ah, inhabitants of the seacoast,
  you nation of the Cherethites!
The word of the Lord is against you,
  O Canaan, land of the Philistines;
and I will destroy you until no inhabitant is left.
6And you, O seacoast, shall be pastures,
  meadows for shepherds
  and folds for flocks.




Ch 2.4-15: Places mentioned in the oracles against foreign nations.




7The seacoast shall become the possession
  of the remnant of the house of Judah,
  on which they shall pasture,
and in the houses of Ashkelon
  they shall lie down at evening.
For the Lord their God will be mindful of them
  and restore their fortunes.


8I have heard the taunts of Moab
  and the revilings of the Ammonites,
how they have taunted my people
  and made boasts against their territory.
9Therefore, as I live, says the Lord of hosts,
  the God of Israel,
Moab shall become like Sodom
  and the Ammonites like Gomorrah,
a land possessed by nettles and salt pits,
  and a waste forever.
The remnant of my people shall plunder them,
  and the survivors of my nation shall possess them.
10This shall be their lot in return for their pride,
  because they scoffed and boasted
against the people of the Lord of hosts.
11The Lord will be terrible against them;
  he will shrivel all the gods of the earth,
and to him shall bow down,
  each in its place,
  all the coasts and islands of the nations.


12You also, O Ethiopians,a
  shall be killed by my sword.


13And he will stretch out his hand against the north,
  and destroy Assyria;
and he will make Nineveh a desolation,
  a dry waste like the desert.


14Herds shall lie down in it,
  every wild animal;a
the desert owlb and the screech owlb
  shall lodge on its capitals;
the owlc shall hoot at the window,
  the ravend croak on the threshold;
  for its cedar work will be laid bare.
15Is this the exultant city that lived secure,
that said to itself,
  “I am, and there is no one else”?
What a desolation it has become,
  a lair for wild animals!
Everyone who passes by it
  hisses and shakes the fist.

title: Zephaniah
text:
3


Ah, soiled, defiled,
  oppressing city!
2It has listened to no voice;
  it has accepted no correction.
It has not trusted in the Lord;
  it has not drawn near to its God.


3The officials within it
  are roaring lions;
its judges are evening wolves
  that leave nothing until the morning.
4Its prophets are reckless,
  faithless persons;
its priests have profaned what is sacred,
  they have done violence to the law.
5The Lord within it is righteous;
  he does no wrong.
Every morning he renders his judgment,
  each dawn without fail;
  but the unjust knows no shame.


6I have cut off nations;
their battlements are in ruins;
I have laid waste their streets
  so that no one walks in them;
their cities have been made desolate,
  without people, without inhabitants.
7I said, “Surely the citye will fear me,
  it will accept correction;
it will not lose sightf
  of all that I have brought upon it.”
But they were the more eager
  to make all their deeds corrupt.


8Therefore wait for me, says the Lord,
  for the day when I arise as a witness.
For my decision is to gather nations,
  to assemble kingdoms,
to pour out upon them my indignation,
  all the heat of my anger;
for in the fire of my passion
  all the earth shall be consumed.


9At that time I will change the speech of the peoples
  to a pure speech,
that all of them may call on the name of the Lord
  and serve him with one accord.
10From beyond the rivers of Ethiopiag
  my suppliants, my scattered ones,
  shall bring my offering.
11On that day you shall not be put to shame
  because of all the deeds by which you
have rebelled against me;
  for then I will remove from your midst
  your proudly exultant ones,
and you shall no longer be haughty
  in my holy mountain.
12For I will leave in the midst of you
  a people humble and lowly.
They shall seek refuge in the name of the Lord—
  13the remnant of Israel;
they shall do no wrong
  and utter no lies,
nor shall a deceitful tongue
  be found in their mouths.
Then they will pasture and lie down,
  and no one shall make them afraid.


14Sing aloud, O daughter Zion;
  shout, O Israel!
Rejoice and exult with all your heart,
  O daughter Jerusalem!
15The Lord has taken away the judgments against you,
  he has turned away your enemies.
The king of Israel, the Lord, is in your midst;
  you shall fear disaster no more.


          16On that day it shall be said to Jerusalem:


Do not fear, O Zion;
  do not let your hands grow weak.
17The Lord, your God, is in your midst,
  a warrior who gives victory;
he will rejoice over you with gladness,
  he will renew youa in his love;
he will exult over you with loud singing
  18as on a day of festival.b
I will remove disaster from you,c
  so that you will not bear reproach for it.
19I will deal with all your oppressors
  at that time.
And I will save the lame
  and gather the outcast,
and I will change their shame into praise
  and renown in all the earth.
20At that time I will bring you home,
  at the time when I gather you;
for I will make you renowned and praised
  among all the peoples of the earth,
when I restore your fortunes
  before your eyes, says the Lord.





1.1: Superscription. Cushi may be either a name or an ethnic designation, “Ethiopian” (see 2.12 and 3.10). If Hezekiah is the eighth-century reformer King Hezekiah (727/715–698/687 bce; 2 Kings 18–20), then Zephaniah was a member of the royal family, which may be indicated by the unusually long genealogy. Josiah (640–609 bce) was also a reformer (2 Kings 22–23), although his father Amon had sacrificed to carved images (2 Chr 33.22).


1.2–18: The coming day of the Lord. 2–3: Punishment is announced against everything on the face of the earth. The language echoes that used in the creation and flood narratives (Gen 1; 6.7; 7.4 and 8.8): everything (lit., “all”); humans (Heb “ʾadam”); face of the earth (Heb “ʾadamah”). God's announcement returns the earth to the destruction announced in Gen 6–7 and overturns the divine promise in Gen 8–9 never again to destroy the earth. 4–5: The language of cut off continues, as God charges Judah's inhabitants with combining worship of the Lord with worship of other deities such as the Canaanite god Baal, the astral deities known as the host of the heavens, and the Ammonite god Milcom. These charges, as well as the term for idolatrous priests, fit well with the accounts of Manasseh's idolatry in 2 Kings 21 and Josiah's reforms in 2 Kings 23; see also Jer 19.13; 32.29. 5: Repetition within v. 5 underscores the duplicity of the people: they bow down and swear both to the host of heaven and to Yahweh. 7–18: The day of the Lord (Joel 1.15; 3.14; Am 5.18; Ob 15; Zech 12.4). Verse 7 introduces vocabulary that will dominate this unit: day appears thirteen times through the end of the chapter. 7–13: The implications of the day for Judah. 7: Be silent, cf. Hab 2.20. Though court officials might be expected to be the guests at the Lord's sacrificial banquet, in an ironic turn they are described as the sacrifice itself. 8–13: A listing of Judah's crimes. 8–9: The linkage between those who adopt foreign attire with those who leap over the threshold, likely a non-Judean religious custom (cf. 1 Sam 5.5), connects assimilation with idolatry. 10–11: The Fish Gate (Neh 3.3; 12.39), the Second Quarter (2 Kings 22.14), and the Mortar (unidentified) likely all refer to wealthy districts in Jerusalem, where traders work. 12–13: Like the fourth-century bce Greek philosopher Diogenes who roamed Athens with a lamp seeking an honest man, the Lord will search Jerusalem with lamps to find the guilty. Because they doubt God's oversight of the world (see also Mal 2.17), their labor will not be successful (see Deut 28.30–31 and cf. Isa 65.21). 14–18: The chapter ends as it began, with attention on all the inhabitants of the earth (v. 18). As elsewhere in the prophets, the day is one of divine wrath (Isa 13.9) from which silver and gold provide no protection (Ezek 7.19). The sins of Judah lead to the destruction of all creation. 15: The term day appears six times in this verse; “Dies irae,” the Vulgate translation of day of wrath, is the title of the well-known medieval sequence for the dead; ruin translates Heb “shoʾah,” a term today used for the Holocaust. Compare Am 5.18–20.


2.1–3: Call to repentance. Although the day of the Lord is imminent, Judah's repentance may yet stave off destruction. 1: The shameless nation likely is Judah. 3: As in Joel 2.14 and Jon 3.8–9, Zephaniah underscores that some could perhaps survive if they seek righteousness (Isa 51.1).


2.4–15: Judgment on the nations. The call for Judah to repent shifts to the announcement that Judah's enemies will be destroyed. 4: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, and Ekron are four of the five major cities of the Philistines (Josh 13.3). Missing from the traditional list is Gath, destroyed by the Assyrians ca. 712 bce. 5: The Cherethites may be synonymous with Philistines (Ezek 25.16; 2 Sam 8.18n.), who ruled the area along the Mediterranean seacoast. 7: Remnant and restore their fortunes may reflect the situation of the Babylonian exile; see also v. 9; 3.18–20n. 8–11: Threats against Moab and the Ammonites, two of Judah's eastern neighbors, are common in prophetic literature (Jer 48–49; Ezek 25; Am 1–2), as is the use of Sodom and Gomorrah to connote total annihilation (Gen 19; Isa 1.9; 13.19; Jer 23.14; 50.4). 9: See v. 7n. 12: The brief mention of the Ethiopians (Heb “Cush,” see 1.1n) seems out of place. 13–15: Assyria, with its capital Nineveh, receives the greatest condemnation, in keeping with the book's Assyrian setting outlined in 1.1. While the translation of the animal vocabulary is difficult, the threat that a city could become the lair for wild animals was common in the ancient world (Isa 13.19–22; 24.11–15). Hisses and shakes the fist, ancient gestures of cursing (Jer 19.8; 49.17; Lam 2.15).


3.1–7: Judgment against Jerusalem. The city Jerusalem is no better than the nations previously judged. Officials, judges, prophets, and priests encompass the entire leadership of the city (Jer 6.13; 14.18). Their deceit sets in contrast the righteousness and just judgments of God. 6–7: God's punishment of the nations should have served as a warning for Judah to fear God and repent (cf. Am 4).


3.8–10: Judgment and salvation of the nations. 8: The day of the Lord, which dominated ch 1, returns; it is here described as a day of God's decision to act against the nations (Joel 3.14). 9: A more universal hope follows, in which all peoples will call on Judah's God (Isa 2; Mal 1.11; Ps 68.31). The punishment of those who built the tower of Babel (Gen 11.9) is reversed. 10: Scattered ones, Judeans who have been exiled to places such as Ethiopia (Heb “Cush”; see 1.1n.; 2.12), will join in this worldwide worship of God.


3.11–13: Salvation in Jerusalem. Focus returns to Jerusalem, for which feminine Heb forms are used. 11: At the time of salvation, God will remove the city's shame (3.19; Joel 2.26–27) and those who are haughty (Isa 2.11,12,17), highly negative terms in prophetic books. My holy mountain, Mount Zion, site of the Temple. 12–13: As in 2.7,9, this verse envisions salvation not for all of Judah but only for a remnant. The humble, those urged in 2.3 to seek righteousness, will survive. Their peaceful state will be like that of guarded sheep.


3.14–20: Salvation of daughter Jerusalem. The feminine characterization of Jerusalem expands to its depiction as a daughter, a designation of the city used throughout the prophets to underscore its vulnerability and utter dependency on God. 15–17: The presence of God as strong king and warrior means that daughter Jerusalem does not need to fear or grow weak (Zech 2.10–11; 9.9–1). 17–18: The Heb is obscure; see textual notes. 17: God the warrior will sing and rejoice, just as Jerusalem was called to do in 3.14. 3.18–20: I will remove disaster from you, contrasting with the beginning of the book, 1.2–3. Restore your fortunes, see 2.7. The deep concern for the ingathering of exiles likely reflects postexilic sentiments, indicating either that these verses were later added to a late-Assyrian-period book or that the book itself was written in the postexilic period as a retrospective look at the time of King Josiah. The language is highly reminiscent of the promises made to Jerusalem in Zech 1–2, as well those made to daughter Zion in Mic 4.6–7, which also envisions the return of the lame and outcast (the same Heb word is translated as “those who were cast off” in Mic 4.7).

title: Lesson 1
text:
How does Matthew begin his gospel account? What does this segment cover?

It begins with a geneology from Abraham to Jesus. It only mentions the men within the family tree until Mary where she is mentioned as the husband of Joseph. I find it interesting that Joseph is mentioned given that Jesus was a product of immaculate conception. Is Joseph actually the father of Jesus, or is Jesus the son of God?




What is covered in this segment?

The birth of Jesus. Joseph discovered that Mary had become pregnant and planned to “dismiss” her (I’m assuming divorce). After receiving a vision of an angel, he decided to the contrary.







What do you learn from these verses about this gospel account?

This a more casual, first-person writing form. The author is writing to his friend Theophilus.




What do these verses cover?

The story of Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth. She was unable to bear children, but an angel appeared to Zechariah explaining that she would give birth, and the child was to be named John, and he would go on to preach and prepare the people for the Lord. Zechariah questioned how he could confirm this to be true, and for his doubt, he was made a mute.
Elizabeth eventually gave birth and said “This is what the Lord has done for me when he looked favorably on me and took away the disgrace I have endured among my people.” The disgrace she suffered was apparently not being able to conceive.




Summarize

The angel, Gabriel, appeared to Mary in this account explaining that she would give birth to Jesus. Mary questioned Gabriel, but he didn’t punish her like he did Zechariah.
Mary met with Elizabeth and her child leapt in her womb. Elizabeth could magically tell that Mary was pregnant with the son of God.
It ends with a poem about How great and merciful God is.




What are the main points in these verse?

Elizabeth gave birth.
The neighbors tried to name him Zechariah at his circumsicion, but Elizabeth said his name is John.
Zechariah said idgaf. It was the first time he had spoken since Gabriel visited him.
Zechariah gave a prophecy that John would become a prophet of God







Who are these verses about and how is he described in verses 1-4, 14, 17-18?

God
1-4: He is both the Word and with the Word.
14: The Word has become flesh (Jesus).
17-18: I honestly don’t know.




Who is the main character in this segment and what do you learn about him?

This segment is about John and his encounter with Jesus. He recognized Jesus as the Messiah on sight alone.




Who takes center stage?

Jesus becomes the focus.







How does Mark start? What’s the first thing you learn from verse 1?

We learn Jesus is the son of God.
It starts with John baptizing in the wilderness when he meets Jesus.

Who is the main character, and what is his message?

John; he says that he baptizes with water but that Jesus will baptize with the Holy Spirit.




What do you learn about Jesus?

Jesus learns that he is the son of God?
